• TETE CZAR'S MESSAGE OF PEACE. The above subject was dealt with by Mr. Smith, oF Ormskirk, on Sunday night, at the Christad,lphiaa Room, Bold-street. The Ler.turer, after giving details of the Reicript, and the present armed condition et soine. of the countries affected by it, coacluded that the Peace Meeting woald be abortive; an i while expressing the Sincerest sympathy with the feeling which prompted the action of those who wiehei for p3aee, he must at the elms time point out the great ignorance displayed by those who expected peace to be brought about by sueh action. There had been peace proposals before. The Prince Consort thought civilisation would accomplish the wok; and in the 48 years which had elapsed eiece the Exhibi• tion, they had not had six consectrive years without a war somewhere on tee earth. Si 111! thoigh7 to bring about peace by commerce ; others hy religioe, the latter also believing that Carist weuld afterwards biern up the earth; a most extraordinary final far a perfected earth. The Psalmist said " It was better to trust in the Llrd than to put confideect in men," and if they wou'd turn tram man to God's Word, they would find that war was be abelished, bet not by a peace Society nor by a man; but by Gol alone, who had reveaied his plan tor the est ablishing of perpetual peace and by searching the scriptures they build that Gad proposed institu;ine a system, which weeld prevent all disputes among nation;. The lord Jest's Christ had enemies who were to be made his footstool and " be mug reign, till he bath out all enemies under his fee." " 'This mat" (Chriw) " shall be the peic " said Micah, and when the Gid of heaven sets up his kingdom which shall never be destroyed" (Din) "The rrince of Peace, of the increa.se of whose government and peace there sh mid be no end" woeld be in th•earth Bing of Kings. Terre would be peace on earrh and glory to Ged in the highest when political and ecclesiastical affairs were in the hands of the sem of God with Christ at their head. They were freely invited ts a participation in the glorious Gospel of the blessed God, and Mr. Smith earnestly urged teem accept the invitation while it WO yet " rft,-3ay."
THE REV. W. H. DRUAMOND AND SUNDAY NEWSPAPERS. .

In Cairo-street Chapel, "en Sunday evening, the Rev. W. H. Drummond, the pastor, preached on' Sunday Newspapers." He seid the severity of the Puritan Sun- day was in accord wit.h ttre severity of it belief in God and its clinging to Scriptural authority. For us that had been modified. Tate reaction aeainst it had not been lead by any great spiritual leader, but prompted rather by a growing laxity and desire to do as they I he 1. So i to many minds tne modern dea of Seri ley wee that of a day of rest and pleasere. Personal disire had taken the place of a divine commend. 'therein ley the danger. The purpcise of Sunday was not merely pleasure— doing as they liked. It was above all a day of rest, a day of remembrance, and these remarks led him to a franls discussion of one of the latest developments of the attempt t break down the customs and the restriellea of Sunday. A short time since two of the great lateidon daily papers announce I that they sveutel begin to issue Sunday editions. Dit,iny people on seeing the annoance- mont were simply horrified without askine themselves why others others treated it RA a matter of indiff.renc', or !night think it would tend to !natio Sunday a little more interesting. But neither attitude was the intelligent one. The issue b3fo:e them was a very grave one— %could the mevement help or hinder thej lenst and the most h-apful use of Sunday ? Would it make life bitter. or would it make it worae ? Suaday wee. made for man, and it was by its u es to the higher life ot man -that all Sunday oteervances mut be jeged. Anything of the kind proposed involved a vest amount of labour. but that was inot the point he wished to emphaeize that 'night. Still t wis right they should rrmemter the amount of machinery which wont have to he -called 'lute i play i. their treat newspepers began putil6h Sunday is: ues. Tee labour invo'ved was out of all compacison. with what would be necwsery in the case of the openine of museums and pineure gat- leries on Sunday—a mevement in which he had always 'taken a great interest ; hecaUt. he believed that the laboer involved would bi very small, would tend to an intelligent use of Sandie, and roh it of some of th, dreariness which mate le a u-eless day to in my 'Wee But they were flee to taco with a very diff irent state of •things when they imagined all ttie activitF of a ereee nowgpeper office going on for seven days instead of see, and the labour involved in the dietributton. P tee movement for Sunday n-warapers suclreJel. if re3ple i supported it and pet the r mosey into it. t would mean an increase of Sunday labour, and Sunday tre:veliine cU over the laud. But let them look at Stiuday in antner 'W.V. What would bi the effccz upon the people, upon them and upon him, if they had their news- papera seven days instead of Fie, if the reading of the morning or evening paper became a poet of their Sunday habit? Was it desirable they sheuld • have their paper on the first day of the werk as on the other sir days? They must not stomplicate the question

by ssauming thet Sunday journalism must necessarily be sensational and of low tone. It might be of a high class tone,though the temptations in the other directions wersuld be very great. There was the world of finance, commerce, politics, anif crime, and it always brought its own labour with it, th-) labour of hard material facts, of dust, aid turmoil. Did they want to live in that world on a Sunday ? Tiler° were three grave reasons for obj-Tting to Siind ay newsp.aper3 and for clohig their best to check the moeement at the outset. First, it would destroy the inea and the passibility of rest. That also had a pile/sir:al side to it; al increasing the terribly nervous strain of modern life, which made so many men prematurely older, and whic i wa, filing their asylums with men W 3030 brains had failed wrier the severe ten- sion of life. An escape frem rens pressure into a calmer atti q deter world for 24 hours was one of the neeative b=nefits of Sunday which thy ceuld nst afford to lose. Mau co lid not de ha week-day work on Sun lay, carry ah iut with him his week-thy anxiety witieue self Ting from it in bdy aad brain. Sscendy, there woald be with that diseppearaec3 ot Sunday as a day of r tst no space left for the higher chines or life. do et much a newspaper with its week- day atausphere w )ul I tend to destry all that. Did they not all feel the value of the atmespher of their English Sunday ? It was something difficult to analyse, but it came week by week with its pee iliar eff,..ct upea heart aad mini, with is sacred aeseciatiens, with its suggestions of qeieter thoughts, with its opportunities for farn!ier interceurse.They could not afford to lean to any- thing whice would make them courser or more material, more unspiritual than they were already. Thirdly, the mutt in time, perhape not in their generation, would be a serious dsteroration of character. Tne rots of hen)ur and duty were in religine. They were vary much what their habit's made them, aid a generation whicn spent its Sunday in pleasure and reading the news- paper werald not be the same as one which acknewleiged, however imperfectly, the obliga- tions and ass yeta-.ione of Sued ay. Did they think that the type would he b tsar or worse ? Turn the ispetion over candidly in their minds. For himself, he could not doubt that it would be infatier.rnere material, less capable of a greet loyalty to the principles of justice and hiremr. He had hot put any theological arguments before them,or any specie' pleadings which some people tboareht it was natural for a minister to speak, but which the ordinary man tna.ted for the most part with indifference. He had wished to appeal to their own serious thought,and he asked them only to put the mat- ter to the test of experience. It was because he believed that Sunday was made for men, and that all its observ- ances might be bet valued by the way in which teey further the beat manhood of men, that he pleaded with them to oppose with all the strength oh serious convic- tiem whatever threatened to rob Sunday ot ite distinc- tiveness, to make i less of a day of rest, and to spell its holy and uplifting associations with the dust and glamour and excitement of the world of toil. They had one day of quiet, that some of its peacefulness migut en- overflew into the six days of laboer. They had one holy day teat ttiey might remember that all their days be- longed to God. Let them beware in the interests of their manhood arid their religion, how they trifled with so pric2less a boon.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, APRIL 28 1899.
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, APRIL 28 1899.
SHOCKING FATALITY TO A. WARRINGTON CARTER.
FATAL JUMP FROM A LURRY.

Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquiry at the Vic- toria Infirmary, Northwich, on Tuesday afternoon, into the circumstances attending the death of George Ryder, a carter, of Warrington, whose death took place in the Institution on Saturchy night, following an accident with which he met about two o'clock in the afternoon, by being run over with a lurry in his charge,at Marston. —Mr. Taylor was foreman of the jury. Mr. C. H. Unsworth, solicitor, Warrington, watched the case on behalf of Mr. Isherwood, the deceased's em- ployer. Ann Elizabeth Ryder, said she resided in Morris-court. off Church-street, Warrington. The deceased was her husband. He was about 50 years of age, and followed the occupation of a carter, being employed by Mr. Isherwood, contractor, Warrington. He had worked for him for three years. He left home at a quarter to six on Saturday morning, and was then well and hearty. He called again at 9.30 to tell her he was going on a journey to Marston, and would return again at 8 or 8.30 p.m. He said four of them were going. He was laugh- ing when he left her, and Ins perfectly sober:. She heard of the accident at four o'clock, and her sons imme- diately came to Norlthwich. She had seen the body, which was that of her bushand.—The Coroner informed the widow that they were all very sorry for her. Robert Kerr, residing at 62, Allen-street, Warringtop, said he was a carter in the service of Mr. Isherwood. His =VT: Vntra9tecl t Wlv beer f9l: the Willereeool Brewery Company. On Saturday morning four of them left Wilderspool with two lurries. He and deceased were in charge of a two horse harry containing 10-i barrels of beer. The deceased was his mate. The other lurry was just behind them. They had to deliver the beer in Northwich and Hartford. Nothing occurred until they reached Marston Bridge. Then the offside chain of the leading horse b?carne uubooked. Both he and the deceased saw it as they were riding on the front part of the lurry. The deceased was eating some bread and butter, and he jumped off to hook the chain. As he did so he said "Go on, we want to get home early." They therefore did not draw up. In getting off the deceased fell. He could not say what caused him to do so. The result was that the off front wheel passed over him. Witness pulled up at once, and prevented the hind wheel doing so. A man in charge of the second lurry, Stephen Beeson, got to him first. He was picked up, but could not stand. They placed him on the lurry between the barrels. Two or three minutes after, Dr. Love, of Great Budworth, came up, and they stopped. He examined the deceased, and ordered them to bring him to the Infir- mary. He hired a trap, and brought him to that institution. On the road the deceased said "It is a bad job it has happened." He appeared to be in great pain. Witness could not say whether he sat wholly on the lurry. There was no rug to trip him. 13e had three glasses of beer on the way—one at Wilder-pool, one at the Cat and Lion, Stretton, and one at the Birch and Bottle at Frandley. He was quite sure that was all toe drink they had. By the Coroner: Were you racing wite the othe turn, ?

Witness ; No, sir. The Coroner : HIW are you paid? Wines: By a weekly wage. The Foreman: Did yuu have a full load on? Witnels : Yes. In answer to a juryman, witness said they were com- ing down a bank near Mr.rAon Schools. Mr. Unsworth : I suppose this was only an ordinary load. You were the drivers and you are an experienced man?

Witness • Yrs, sir. Mr. Unsworth : Is it not a regular practice for carters to jump off the lorries when in motion ? Witness : Yes, sir. Mr. Unswortr : Did you offer to pull up when the chain came off ?
Witness: I had not time beton tha deceased jumped off.

J,..bn Arnold, Warrington, said he was a carter for Mr. Isherwood, and was in charge of the second lurry, on Saturday. When opposite Marston Schools the first bury stopnetand he got off to see what was Vas matter. Ho then bound the deceased lying on the ground clear of the lurry. He did not know the wheel had gone over him. He said to witnes, "This means another six weeks in the Infirmary for me." Wimess could see he was badly hurt. He assisted to place him on his lurrv. A few minutes later Dr. Lowe drove up, and witness stopped him. He examined the man, bandaged him up, and told them to bring him to the Infirmary. Witness found the chain of the leading horse of; the first lurry unhooked.
The Coroner : Bad you got on the trot aftPr coming down tbe
Witaess : No, sir. The Coroner: Was there any larking going on? Witness : No, sir. The Coroner : Firm, many glasses of beer had he to drink during the day.

Witness: Three.- 'By Mr. Unsworth : In your experietre has a chain of .hat particular pattern ever bacome unhookel ? Witness : Ido not use tham. Mr. Unsworth : Do you think it is a safe kind ? Witness : Yes, sir.

Stephen Beeson, living at Spring Bridge, Wildersnool, also a carter, sal.] he was with the witness Arneld on Slturday. He was driving the second furry. When near Marston Schools they saw deceased on the ground, and they ran to his assistance.

IO answer to the Coroner, witness said they were not racing, nor trotting. In answer to Mr. Unsworth, vritness stated he had used that particular kind of chain, and he had knswn thrm to erraP rff. It was a rezolar custom for carters tosjamp off lorries when they are moving.

Matsu Baia the deceased .ai dnu'ited to the In- firmary shortly after three o'clock, on Saturday after- noon. He attended him. On examination he found a compound fracture of the right leg, and several long clean cut wounds on the same leg. The right collar bone bone was broken, and one of the ends had been driven into the lung. He was suffering very much from shock, and had great difficulty in breathing. He saw him again about six o'clock, having previously done all that was possible. He then found him better as far as the shock was concerned, but the breathing was worse. The The cause of death was asphixia. The piece of the broken collar bone which had penetrated the lung, had caused it to collapse, whereby the air was forced all over the body under the times of the skin. It was a very rare injury, and hardly any such eiseo were recorded in medical books.

In answer to the Coroner, witness said the deceased was perfectly sober. Redid not question him abaut the accident, but did all be could to ',neve his intense pain. Continuing Dr. Marsh said the deceased died about a quarter to ten o'clock. He knew the case was hopeless from the first.

The Coroner in summing up bald he did not think the three glasses of b,er which deceased had had during the day were too much for such a man during that period. Re thought KPrr deferved every praise for stopping the lurry before the second wheels passed over the body,and they might fairly assume that the other men, judging from their actions, had their heads screwed on all right. Fortunately one of them saw Dr. Love and stopped him. The cause of death was perfectly apparent, and it was for them to say whether anybody was to blame or not. He felt that no blame whatever could be attached to Mr. Isherwood, ;Ole evidently did his best to provide his workmen with the best materials.
The Foreman said he knew the deceased very well. He had been in the habit of callinz at his hous., and he always found him a very steady and industrious man.

The jury returnel vercliot in accordance with the medical evidence to the effect that deceased died from asphyxia—suffocation. Mr. Uns worth said he was please] to inform them that Mr. Ithervrocd, thouch not entertaining any liability, had decided to defray the co3t of the funeral of the deceased.
The Coroner :_ I am very pleased to hear that.

By JOHN DLOUNDELLE-BURTON, Author of " Fort une's 1117 'PO e, " "The Scourge of God," "Across the 'Salt Seas," "The. Clash of Arms," "In the Day of Adversity," "A Gen- tleman Adventurer," "His Own Enemy," "Denounced," &L.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDINU CHAPTERS: Arabella Waldron, a young aid, is to sail for India in a ship belonging to her uncle, Captain Pooley, in order to be married at Bombay. But ,previously the reader is to be told of her courtship. A year before,•the Captain had taken her to the theatre; where she had met Stephen Charke, a young friend of her uncle, who is smitten by her. Afterwards, at a lunch at Portsmouth, Bella. meets .Gilbert Bampfyld, a flag-lieutenant to the: Rear-Admiral, and at a ball in the trreyi g she 'gives him most of her dances.
MUTTER T,
SO, FAIMY:CLT, 13 !

Nine months had tersed since' • the entertainment of the foreign fleet at Portsmouth—months that had been pregnant with events cohcerning• the three .persons With whom' this intrratire deals ; and .Bella sat now, at the end of a dull March f afternoon, in the pretty deawing-rosee in Weft Kensington. Sat there-tneeitaing aoqly,. einee she happened to be alone at the moment, owing to Mrs. Waldron having gone out to pay several calls.. Of all who had b'en at those entertainments,' of al in the party which, in the preceding June, had gathered together at Portsteoeth, the three ladies of the ,family, Mrs.- Waidren, Mrs. Pooley and Bella, were alone in -Eitel:and ; the three! 'men— the three sailors—were all gone to :different parts of the world. Captain Pooley had sailed with his vessel te Australia; Stephen Charke had gone to China as first officer a a large vessel and Gilbert Bampfyld, Who, in consequence ' of the Rear- Admiral's retirement, no longer wore the aigaillettes of a flag-lieutenant, • had.. been appointed to the Brisetts, nn the East Indian station. And Bella, sitting now in her arm-chair in front of, the drawing-room fire, with a letter lying open on her lap before her, was thinking of the writer of that letter, as well as of all that it contained. If one glances at it as it lies there before her, much may be gleaned of what has hap- pened in those nine months ; while perhaps, also, some idea, some light, may be gained of that which is to come. - "My darling," it cee.t-e!d--and possibly the writer, far away, may have hoped that, as he wrote those words, they would be kissed as often by the person to whom they were addressed as he fondly desired—"my darling—Your letter came to me to- day, and I r list write back to you at once—this very instant—not only because I want to put all my thoughts on paper, but also because .I can thus catch the P. and 0. mail. How good! how good you are! Also, I do not forget. how goed your mother is. I know I ought not—at. least, I suppose I ought not—to ask you to do such a thing as come out to me, and I can assure you I hesitated for weeks before &ring to do so. Yet, when I reflected that, if you could not bring yourself to come, as well as induce your mother to give her consent to your coming, we could not possibly be married for three years, I could not hesitate any longer. And now—now-0 Bella, my darling! I could dance for joy if rer. c tbin was. big ,enough to allow of such a !1‘ ne—you are coming! You will come! How ha r' W shall be! I can think of nothing else—n• thing. You don't know how I feel, and it's useless for me to try to tell you , . • • • No more need be read of this letter, however, ard, since the reader will shortly be informed of what led to it, nothing more need be said than that, after a good deal of explanation as to how the young lady fn whom it was addressed was to make her pi ms for reaching Bombay, it was signed , "Gilbert Pampryld." 1 So that one sees now what had been the outcome of that N, (a,‘k of delight at Portsmouth during the • last smumer ; one understands all that had been the ;result of, those garden-parties and that ball. 91a,y—the festivities—were followed by a re- newal of the acquaintanceship between Mrs. Waldron and her daughter and Gilbert Bampfyld, aq, indeed, the latter had quite made up his mind _ _ .

should be the case; and as--Since the truth must i always be snoken—Bella had hoped would happen. They were followed, that is to say, directly the naval manoeuvres were over, for which important function both divisions of the Channel Squadron were of course utilised, while not a week had elapsed from , the time of the return of the ships to their stations ' before Gilbert Bampfyld presented himself in 1, Montmorency-road. And that presentation of him- self at this saburban retreat was, it is surely unnecessary to say, succeeded by many other things, all showing what was impending and what actually happened later on. Gilbert Bampfyld told Bella that he lbved her and wanted her for his wife, and —well! one can imagine the rest. What was there to stand between those two loving hearts? What? Nothing to impede their engagement; nothing that need have impeded their immediate marriage, except the fact that Bella's maiden modesty could never have bee' brought to consent to a union so hurriedly entered into as would have been necessary had the agreed to become Gilbert's wife ere he set out for Bombay to join the Mriseus, to which he was now appointed. One regrets, however, when describing such soft and glowing incidents as these that space is so circumscribed (owing to the canvas having to be filled with larger events now looming near) as to leave no room for more minute description of this love idyl. It would have been pleasant to have dwelt upon Bella's ecstatic joy at having been asked to be the wife of the one man—the first man—whose love she had ever desired—(ah ! that is it—to be the first man—the first girl—who has ever touched the Iheart of him or her we worship) ; only it must not be—the reader's own imagination must be asked to I fill the missing description. Let those, therefore, who remember the earliest whispered word of love they ever spoke or had spoken to them • who recall still the first kiss they ever gave or took; and can remember also all the joy that came to them when first they loved and knew themselves- beloved, fill the Hatus. That will suffice. "We shall be so happy, dearest," Gilbert said, when all preliminaries had been arranged in so far as their engagement was concerned, and when he did not know at the time that he was about to be sent on.foreign service, but hoped that he would !either be allowed to remain in the Channel , Squadron or be transferred to the Training Squadron, or, at worst, appointed to the Mediter- ranean. "We shall be so happy, darling. I hoped from the first to win you--though—though some- times I feared there might be someone else." "There could never have been anyone else. Never, after I had once met you," she murmured. "0, Gilbert!" and then she too said she was so

happy. Yet a moment later she whispered: "Yet, somehow, it seems too good to be true. All has come so easily in the way that I—well, as we— desire d that sometimes I think there may be— that something may arise to—to---" "Whet—prevent our marriage? Nothing can do that. Nothing could have done that—nothing I " "Seppose your uncle, Lord D'Abernon, had objected," she said, remembering that she had herd how this nobleman was not always given to making things quite as easy and comfortable to those by whom he was surrounded as was considered desirable. "Suppose that had happened ? " "Oh! he's all right," Gilbert replied. "He expected his opinion to be asked and his consent obtaired, and all that sort of thing, but outside that he's satisfied. And if he wasn't, it wouldn't have in tde any difference to me—after I had once seen you." For which remark he was rewarded with one of those chaste salutes which Bella had learnt by now to bestow without too much diffidence. As regards Mrs. Waldronwell! she was a mother, and it was not to be supposed that such a distinguished match as Bella was about to make could be aught but satisfactory to her; while Captain Pooley, who had not yet departed with the Emperor of the Moon for Australia, told his niece that she was a lucky girl. He also informed Gilbert that, as he was a childless man, Bella would eventually fall heiress to anything he and his wife might leave behind them. Mkters looked, there- fore, as though they would all go merry as the proverbial marriage bell. All, as the old romancists used to say, was very well. • Then fell the first blow—the one that was to separate those two fond hearts. Gilbert was sud- denly appointed to the •Brisetis and ordered to proceed to Bombay to join her at once, and, a fortnight later, he was gone, and poor Bella was left behind lamenting. She was sitting, lamenting still, before her fire on this March day, with this newly-arrived letter on her lap—in solemn truth, she had been lamenting his departure ever since it had taken place—when suddenly there broke in upon her ears the sound of

mvzsitors Knock below. "nen, ere elle COUla anr- tinguish whose voice it was addressing the servant who had answered the door, she heard a manly footstep on the stairs, and, a moment later, the maidservant announced: "Mr, Charke." Mr. Charke! the man whose memory bad almost fadea from her mind—as she had reproached herself more than once when it did happen to recur to her —the man whom she had learnt to like so much during all that happy time last year. Now, as she gazed on him as he. came forward, and noticed how brown he was—more deeply browned, indeed, than she had thought it possible for him, who was already so tanned and sunburnt, to be—and noticed, too, the strong, self-reliant look on his face, she reproached herself again. She acknowledged, also, that she had liked him so Much that 'even her nelt. found happiness ought not to have driven all recol- lection of him entirely from her mind. Then she greeted him warmly, saying all the pleasant little words of welcome that a woman whose heart goes in unison with her good" breeding knows how to say, and made him welcome. Yet, as she did so, she noticed that he was graver, more sad, it seemed to her, than she had ever repwteil before. - _ _

"You aro notill?" asked,' as this fact became more and more apparent to her. "Surely you, a sailor, have not come back from the sea unwell? At least, I hope not." "No," he said, "no, Nor, I hope, do I seem so? Do you know that, besides any desire to call and see you, I came for another purpose," an`d. now his eyes rested on hr with so strange a light —so mournful, deep, a light—that in a moment her woman's instinct told her something Its plainly as though his voice had done so. Like a flash of lightning, that instinct revealed to her the fact that this man loved her; that, from the moment they had parted, months ago, she had never been absent from his mind. She knew it; she was certain she was right—she could not be deceived! Then to herself she said: "Heaven help him—Heaven prevent him from telling me so." _ _

But aloud, her heart full of pity, she id:sa "Indeed," and smiled bravely on him while she spoke. "Indeed; what was that purpose ? " "To congratulate you. To— " Congratulate me!" "Yes. I met the Emperor of the Moon at Cape- town. We were both homeward bound. And— and—your uncle told me the news. I offer my con- gratulations now." Yet, as he said the words, she saw that his face was turned a little aside; she could not perceive his eyes. Congratulations! Well, they might be sincere in so far as that, because he loved her, he wished her well, desired that she should be happy, but—but—otherwise—no! it was not to be thought upon. As he said the words: "I congratulate you," he followed an old 'custom—one more foreign than English—and held out his hand, taking hers, and he. kept it, too, fast in his own, while he said, in the voice that his struggles with the elements had made so deep and sonorous: "Yes, congratulate you. I must do that. To— to—see you happy—to know you are so, is all that I have—all—l hope for now. Yet there is no treachery to him in what I say. God help me! I mean none—but—but—l—from the first—l have

"No! no!" she murmured, striving to withdraw her hand, yet not doing so angrily. "No, no. Don't say it, Mr. Charke. Don't, pray don't." And, now, neither could he see her eyes nor her averted face. "Don't say it. You do not desire to make me unhappy ? " she murmured. "Never, as God hears me. But—l have said it. I had to say it. Good-bye." "Good-bye," she said,—and then, as he neared the door, she turned once and looked at him with eyes that were full of infinite pity and compassion.
CHAPTER VI.
"AND BEND THE GALLANT MAST, MY BOYS."

Events are now drawing near to that night when Bella was to have these distressing dreams which have been mentioned at the opening of this narrative; all was arranged for her departure to Bombay. A little more, and she will be on her way to India and to wedlock. .

_ Yet all had not been quite easy and smooth in the settlement of affairs. At first Mrs. Waldron, good, loving mother though she was, and fully cogni- sant of the facts—namely, that Bella loved Lieutenant Bampfyld madly and would be an unhappy woman if she did not become his wife long ere three years had passed, and that the match which her child was about to make was undoubtedly a brilliant one—refused to hear of such a thing as that she should go out to him. "If you are worth having," she said, when first the proposal was submitted to her, "you are surely worth coming for." And, since this was a truism, it was hardly to be gainsaid. Yet, as we know by now, she had been won over by her daughter's pleadings and entreaties; by, too, the plain and undeniable fact that there was not the slightest possibility of Lieutenant Bampfyld being able to come home to marry her, or to return to England in any way—short of being invalided—until the Briseus herself returned.

Then, no sooner had this difficulty been sur- mounted, than another reared its head before mother and daughter. How was she to go out to Bombay alone and unprotected? A young married woman, who had to proceed to India to join her husband, might very well undertake such a journey, but not a young woman such as Bella was, while for chaperon or protectress there was no one forth- coming. At first, it is true, Mrs. Waldron had meditated on accompanying Bella herself (she being an old sailor, to whom long sea voyages were little more than railway journeys are to some more stay- at-borne ladies) ; only, down in the depths of her nature, which was an extremely refined one, there was some voice whispering to her that it would be indelicate to thus brine' her daughter out in pursuit of her affianced husband. It is true, however, that authorities on social etiquette who have since been consulted have averred that this was a false feeling which was in possession of Mrs. Waldron's mind; but, be that as it may, it existed. Also, she still regarded the matter of her child going to her husband, instead of that husband coming to fetch her, as one of particular delicacy; one of such nicety as to permit of no elaboration; and she resolved that, come what might—even though she should have to purchase, or hire rather, the services of an elderly and austere travelling com- panion—she must not herself accompany Bella. "Heaven knows what is to be done, she said to her daughter, as they discussed the important point, "but I suppcse it will come to that," the "that" meaning the hired chaperon. Then she sighed a little, remembering how the late Captain Waldron had encompassed thousands of miles in a voyage which he made from the Antipodes to espouse her. Yet, ere many days had passed, the clouds of obstruction were suddenly removed in a, manner which seemed almost—as the fond nr!:-,her stated— providential. Captain Pooley's ship ha.l, followed home, after a week or so of interval, .that in which Stephen •Charke had returned to England, and its arrival was soon succeeded by his own at &out- morency-road. "Going out to him to be married!" he exclaimed, after his sister—who happened to be alone at the time of his visit—had made him acquainted with what she had given her consent to some two or three months before, on Gilbert's application backed up by Bella's supplications, and which she had moaned over inwardly ever since she had so given it. "Going out to be married, eh? Why! she must want a husband badly!" Yet, because he.knew well enough the customs of Her Majesty's Service and the impossibility which prevailed in that Service of an officer corning home to marry his bride, he did not repeat her words, "If she is worth having, she is worth coming for." "So other people have thought, if they hs.ve not openly said so," Mrs. Waldron replied. "I am sure they, must have thought so. Yet," she went on, with determination, "I have agreed to it, and I cannot retract my word. It is given, and must be kept. No, it is not that which troubles me." "What, then? "

"Why, the getting out. How is the child to go alone, in a great liner, with two or three hundred passengers, all the way to Bombay? How ? " she repeated. "Bombay, eh? Bombay. Oh! well, if that's her destination, she can go comfortably enough. There need be no trouble about that. Only, she will be more than double the time the P. and 0., or any other line, would take to carry her." "What do you mean, George ? " "Why," he said, "I happen to be taking the old Emperor to Bombay next month with a general cargo—calling at the Cape on the way. She can go with me, and welcome. There's a cabin fit for a duchess which she can have."

It was a cabin fit for a duchess, as Bella and her mother acknowledged when, a fortnight later, they went down to Gravesend to inspect the Emperor of the Moon, and after it had been decided 'in inlemn family conclave that by this ship the former

, abolia maKe tne voy,i2-0o ILUa. Also, it was more than likely.that the girl would make it.under par- ticularly pleasant circiunstances, since this was one of those occasions on which Mrs. Pooley had decided to accornisany her husband, she not baTing felt very well during the past winter. At present the cabin was empty and denuded of everything, Pooley having decided to have it refurnished; but when he told them how that furniture would be arranged in ,the great roomy . place, which would have been 'dignified as a "state-room" in one of the old clippers, Bella again said, as. she had said sO often before, that "he was the best old uncle in , the world."

Now, the Emperor of the Moon was a smart, though old-fashioned, full-rigged ship of about silk hundred tons, her lines being perfect, yet leaving Uet full of room inside. Her saloon was a corattrF.able one; well furnished with plush-coveted chairs and benches—the covering being quit,,, new; a piano— also looking new—was lasb.e'l to the stem of the mizzenmast, while thVe were swinging vases, in which latter, no ileubt, fresh ferns Sad flowers ro:4ld be placod. On deck she was very clean and white, with "much bras 3 and everything neat and shipshape, while the seaman who should regard her bows and stern would at once acknowledge that she left lit.±l9 to desire, old as she was. For they built ships in tho clays when she was laid with a view to both sea qualities rfnd comfort, and the Emperor of the Moon lacked neftber. Her sleeping- cabins were bedrooms, her saloon wasa dining- room as good as you would find in a Afty..nound- a year suburban residence, and her masts riraid have done credit to one of Her Majesty's earlier ships.. _ . .

Altogether, Della was pleased with everything, espe- cially with her cabin, which was on the port side of the saloon, and, besides, was pleasantly excited at the idea of so long a sailing voyage. "I know,'" she said to her uncle, "that we shall have a delightful time of it, and for companionship I shall have you and auntie. That's enough." "You will have someone else, too," Pooley said, with a smile "you know I have two officers. Come "—and again he smiled—"it is our log days,' " by which he meant that they were shipping their ctir,o. "Come, and I will introduce them to you." Then he led the way up the companion to the deck. _

They met one of these officers, the secondsmate, a young man whom Pouley introduced, as Mr. Fagg, and then, while they were all talking together, Bella •heard a deep, low voice behind her say: "How do you do, Miss Waldron ? " A 'voice that caused her to start as she turned round to find herself face to face with Stephen Charke. "You!," she exclaimed involuntarily. "You! Are you going on this voyage ? " "I am first officer," he said. "I wanted a berth, and Captain Pooley has given me one." And amidst her uncle's joyous laughter and his remark that he knew this would be a pleasant surprise for Bella, and while, too, Mrs. Waldron said that she was delighted to think he would be in the ship to look after her daughter, that daughter had time to think—to reflect. In her heart she would far rather that Chalice had not been here; also, she wondered how he could have brought himself to accept his present position, knowing, as he must have known, that she was going in the ship. "It is so vain, so useless," she thought; "and can only lead to discomfort. We shall both feel embarrassed all the way. Oh! I wish he were not coming." Then, although she pitied him, and although she had always liked him, she resolved that through the whole of the time they were together in the ship she would see • as little of Stephen Charke as possible. "You do not object to my presence, I hope ? " he said a moment later, as they both stood by the capstan alone—Pooley and his wife and sits's', having moved off forward. "I should be sorry to think my being here was disagreeable to you. I have to earn my living, you know." "What right could I have to object, Mr. Charke ? " "Perhaps you think I have behaved indis- creetly ? " For a moment she let her eyes fall on him and rest upon his own; then she said: "I will not give any opinion. You have to earn your living, as you say; while as for me—well, you know what lam going to India for." "Yes," he answered. "I do know." After which he added: "Do not be under any wrong impression. I shall not annoy you. lam the chief officer of this ship and you are a passenger. That is, I understand, how the voyage is to be made ? " "If you please," Bella replied very softly, and the tones of her voice might well have brought some comfort to him, if anything short of the possession of her love could have done so. A fortnight or three weeks, later, the pilot had left the Emperor of the Moon, the lee main braces were manned, the ship was lying over under her canvas, the wind was well astern. Bella was on 1, her way to India and her lover! Let us pass over the parting between mother and child, the fond embraces, the tears and sobs which accompanied that parting following after the dawn when we first made the girl's acquaintance. Following, too, that night of unrest and disturbing dreams. No description of such partings are necessary; many of us. young and old, men and women, have had to make them ' • to part from the loved grey-haired mother who has s. Mxid on our breast ere we went forth to find our livelihood, if not our fortune, in a strange world; many of us have had to let the child of our longings and our hopes and prayers go forth from us who have shel- tered and nurtured it—us who have perhaps prayed God night and day that, in His mercy, it might never leave our side. We go away ourselves because we must; also they go from us because they must,- and there is nothing but the same hope left in all our hearts—the hope that we shall not be forgotten —that, as the years roll by, those we have left behind will keep a warm spot for us in their memory, oz. that those who have left us behind will_ sometimes turn their thoughts back longingly to us in our clesolatio-s. It has to be, and it has to be borne; alas! that parting is the penalty we all have to pay for has ing ever been permitted to be together. And so across the seas the stout old Emperor of the Moon went, buffetissg with the Channel, throwing aside the rough waves with her forefoot as though she despised them, sinking England and home behind her with every plunge she made. And at the moment that sh was leaving the , Lizard far away astern of her, and was running well out into the Atlantic, a telegram was delivered in Montmorency-road addressed to Bella, which was opened by her mother. A telegram signed "Gilbert," which ran: "Don't start. Briseus appointed to East Coast Africa, slaver catching." A telegram that had come three days too late! A telegram that was re-forwarded to Capetown. where it lay for forty-seven days awaiting the arrival of tb4 Emperor of the Moon, and then—was forgotteis (To be continued.) DR. BAUNARDO'S HOMES. Special meetings on behalf of the above homes are to be held in Parr Hall, Warrington, next week. The bounder of these grand institutions that have done so much good for the Waifs and Strays of the Kingdom commenced his life's work thirty-two years ago in Stepney, and then over 35,000 poor wastrels, chiefly orphans,thrown on the cold mercY of the world, have passed through the Barnard° Homes, and been educated and trained to fill useful positions in life. At present there are 5,000 childrea in the Homes and Branches. Dr. Barnard° is carrY- ing on a truly national work, and deserves the practital sympathy and support of all who have the interests of c; ildren at heart. What be has saved to the country at large by his successful reclarrie tion of waifs is beyond computation, and we there; fore invite attention to our advertising coluninseana trust that the cordial support of the residents of Warrington will Be given to the meetings. Further particulars will be fouad in our alvertisia columns.

LADIES' LETTER
MY DEAR NELLIE,

Just at present the rage is for millinery, se I cannot do better than write to you on some very fancy selection of hats—hats for the park, hats for the street, for the morning and the afternoon, hats for the cycle and the tennis court, for the river and the golf links, hats severe therefore, and hats gay and charming, with tulles and flowers and sweep- ing plumes, and there are some half-dozen or so of picturesque hats and pretty jaunty toques. The sumptuous headgear with the toque all herissd with chiffon and tulle, rather than the sterner section is reserved for the morning costume and, for sports. That toque, for example, which massed with cerise chiffon has tucked into its most becoming brim clusters of small shaded damask roses. Frankly, some woman, she with the colour- ing that asks for this dark warm pink, will bless me for ever for pointing out to her that little toque. It is a fact that a woman's fate has ere this lurked in a bonnet, or a toque. She who, on the otlier hand, delights in a pinkish mauve will be sweet on the mauve straw toque, that on the uplifted left side of its double brim is entirely covered with tucked and rucked mauve chiffon and boasts a cluster of purple pansies for its finish. She of dark hair will like to poise upon it that toque of maiz 3 and white tulle whose draped brim is crossed by loops of maize straw, and of which the centre is two giant maize roses, and the side flaish a big black rose and pale green foliage.

She who affects the picturesque will immensel3 fancy that hat of black crinoline straw, from the front of which sweep three big black and white plumes. It is an extremely smart hat. She might also with much charm affect that boldly uplifted toque of drawn tulle over white on which jet cabochons stud the brim, and three plumes jauntily start from a big buckle. And yet another is that picturesque hat of somewhat Trelawney build, that is covered all over with drawn tuchs of white tulle draped over on the brim by clear black Chantilly lace, and finished on the left side by bows of black velvet, and blaek-and-wbite Paradise feather. A most charming thing in silver straw is yet another of these that has lovely shaded grey tips at the side, and a draping of tulle to support the folds of this quaint and lovely straw. A cycling hat which I have seen is of natural Panama, with a very smart fan bow in shaded tones of turquoise is most sermt for the cycle. Having said enough of toques and millinery will turn my attention to other departments of attire. There are some very tasty costumes in serge, one being a very neat and serviceable model, which can be made in navy blue and cream.
I

Velours du Nord can be cut in a similar manner, with each part running the same way of the stuff. Before cutting out, the velvet must be carefully tested, holding first one end and then the other. One way there will be light shades on looking down the velvet, and the other will have a dense rich black, and this latter should be marked as the top, and all the top pArts of the pattern kept to this end. The most economical method of cutting the velvet is when the large upper part .of the sleeve is not cut from ths top, and an extra quantity of velvet is required to make the coat. The sleeve, by being placed above the smallest side-piece, equalises the length, and less stuff is required. Toe silk lining is cut the same as the velvet, and joined up separately in three parts. 'When the velvet seams are all sewn and opened, a strip of whalebone is an improvem*ut at the t esom gores and under-aria seam.

There are some very smart walking dresses to be seen, one was a very smart little cat of black Cloth, which is cut up in front in a very becoming style, and has a long habit back. The revers and cuffs are faced with material to match the skirt, and there are rows of small &met buttons on either side. This can be made in .4hocks of any colour, with cloth goats to match. A very smart walking dram in the tailor made style, made of soft beige coloured stuff, had the front width of the skirt male wi:11 the sides coin- ing over it in round scallops, edged with raised brown braid. The jacket Hid two little habit tabs at the back, and round scallops in front all edged with the fancy braid. A. coloured fancy silk plastron was put in lieu of waistcoat. A high velvet collar was of a zrullierry brown shade' and the top of the sleeves and wrists were finished with this velvet and rows of thb braid. This skirt was lined. The other ones of thin material were made over silk underskirts. .

stores of our elders can often be made to yield us. One of the latest subjects of statistical inquiry is the eyes, light and dark. It has been discovered that taking the average of Europe and America, 446 is the percemt- age of men having light eyes, includimg blue and grey, The proportion of girls and womer. having blue or grey eyes is, by the same computation 342 per cent. In other words, blue eyes are decidedly rarer among women than among men. Men have light eyes oftener than women, but in the int,rmediate grade of colour between light and dark, th- percentage of the two sexes is verp nearly the same. In this in.ermediate category are brown and hazel eyes, neither pure light nor genuine black. The percentage of those among (Lien is 43'1, and among women 451.. The p.rcentage of dark, or more properly, black eyes is larger among women, being 20.7 per cent of the whole number, while among men it is 12 3. In Southern European countries, dark eyes bate among men and women predominate. while light eras are to bo found in jus; as high a propor- tion in Northern countries. "WOMEN'S CHIT."

At Windsor, preparations for Her Majesty's return are , in full swing. The dismantled private apartments are weuming the aspect customary to them when the Queen is in residence, and Si soon as the favourite pieces of furniture, bric-a-brac, mementoes of family and friends which always accompany the Sovereign on her travels, reach the Castle, they will be unpacked, and arranged in their usual postions before the Queen arrives. Her Majesty possesses a most retentive memory and the arrangement of her personal surroundings is ex- ceedingly conservative. The Queen's favourite portion of the grounds at Wind- sor is that known as the "Slopes." The path broken up into nooks, so to speak, winds through woodland, up hill and down dale, and here and there among greenery ap- pear white headstones by miniature graves. The favourite dogs of Her Majesty are thus honored by tokens of her remembrance. Though much of the gold and silver plate at Windsor is, like the Crown jewels, Crown property,the Queen can claim nearly half a million pounds worth as her own. A splendid piece is the rose water fountain designed by H,sßoyat Highness the late Prince Consort. The size of the fountain at the base is some four feet square, and it is about the same in height. The weight is no less than 2,380 ounces. Another piece of great interest as the silver font which was used for the christening of all the Royal children. It was manufactured in 1840, and has been in use for the same purpose ever since. The Queen's pictures and statuary bold perhaps value that is more sentimental than monetary,but much of the china, bronze, and knick-knacks, which she has purchased are intrinsically worth a very great deal. Lady ()erica Duncombe's engagement to the Bishop of Stepney has caused no surprise among her friends and acquaintances. She has never cared for society, and from the time she was presented until now has avoided the gay round of balls, dinners etc., as much as possible. She is in every way fitted to become a clergyman's wife, and after her marriage intends to devote her life to work among the very poor. Lady Ulrica is, like all her sisters, very beautiful. Her fiance is about forty. He was educated at Keble College, and ordained in 1884. Eleven years later he bezame the Rector of Bethnal Green, and was consecrated Bishop of Stepney in 1897. Thereare few who have any idea of what it costs to ,be married in style. Take the cost of the carriages. In fashionable society this is semetimes a serious item. Orie of the biggest orders on record was that given by a cer- tain Colonel who was married from the Langham Hotel, London. He had thirty-seven carriages each with a pair of horses, and coachman and footman, and for these he bartered the noble sum of £lOO. A fashionable carriage provider, without whose aid very few society weddings in London take place, recently announced that a canines and pair, with toetman ant coachman coats three guineas, and other carriages £2 ss. 6J. With regard to the flowers,frequently as muah as £5O to £BO is spent on bcquets alone, the orange blossoms being transmitted from Nice and Genoa. Then there anethe dresses, and last but by no means least, the pre- sents. The Dowager Duchess of Newcastle's presents in gems alone amounted to £lOO,OOO in value. A shaele head ornament was assessed at no less than £15,000, and there was a single diamond which would have taken the purchasing power of £B,OOO or £lO,OOO to buy. The Marquis of Bath's gift to his bride was worth £30,000 and it may not be generally known that the most valu- able row-of pearls in the world was given to Lady Tweedmouth on her marriage. No pains or expense were spared to ensure the purity and perfectness of the gems,correspendence being carried on all over the world to secure a gift which should be absolutely unique. It cost between £B,OOO and £lO,OOO. Turquoises may be seen in profusion just now, at all leading jewellers. Single turquoises between the links of a fine gold chain is a novelty in necklac s, while tur quoise tassels are a feature of the newest bangles. Gold- curb bracelets are set with turquoises, and aigerettes tipped with this favourite stone, to bring them up to date. As to whether the palm should be given to the Empress of Russia's collection of turquoises,or to that of Baroness-Coutts, experts are doubtful. The former has been accumulating her treasures for years, and would see= despite her serious disposition to believe in some of the properties attributed to them by legend. Her betrothal ring consisted of a matchless turquoise, and since the Czar first gave it to her she has never taken it off, and she declares that she never will do so. There is a Russian proverb to the effect that a turquoise given by a loving hand carries with it happiness.safety, and good fortune. The poorest peasant girl mu,t have a turquoise in her engagement rieg if she would expect happiness. And once this engagement ring is on the finger she must never part with it, if she would keep the faith and affectioh of her betrothed. The Shah of Persia pcesesses some very fine stones.so does Lady Warncliffe, one ef whose beautiful speeimens is engraved with a mystic inscription in Persian characters. The largest flawless turquoise owned by any private person, is the -property of the Duchess of Wsstminster. The white tulle bow beneath the chin is still worm by up-to-date women,but unless one's dress allots auce is of goodly proportions it is well toavoid this idea altogether. Tulle is undoubtedly expensive wear. It serves bat once, utterly declining to !Sok anything but simply squalid on being asked to tie itself a second time. Fall ties are better, but not much. They soon lose their freshness, and when that is lost, all is lost. Little bolero jackets are, being built to match tailor- made skirts, and these are usually lined with a pale coloured brocade. Cut away in front, the newest have two pendant narrow ends from the neck to below the waist, which are finished with fringed tassels, and lined like the bolero. Soft' chiffon or muslin blouses are sup- plied to match, or blend with, the lining of the bolero, and the two make a change from the warmer 'cut and waistcoat which we can now dispense witi when the still

shines. The blouse of to-day is as elaborare as one likes to make it. The. omnipotent tuck appears everywhere. metimes it is vertical and arranged in graups. At others, transverse, forming a yoke, or extending from neck to waist. One very effective plan for the front of a Was° ot thin cotton or muslin, is to run severtl rows of tucks with strong thread, and then gather them up to form. a kind of ruching. The übiquitious ohemisette adapts itself to the ornamental blouse as happily as to other bodices, only it is always of mousieline de soie, or plain Indian muslin. div.head: WARRINGTON RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB. A REVIEW OF THE SEASON.
div.p: WARRINGTON RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB. A REVIEW OF THE SEASON.

It is not with the pleasantest feelings that I sit down to review the doings of the Warrington Foot- ball Club during the season just drawing to a close. The task would be ever so much easier and pleasanter had I to chronicle mighty deeds and brilliant performances such as used to be associated with football in Warrington, but which have been almost entirely conspicleas by their absence since the inception of the Northern Union. This organisa- tion has made competition between the clubs of Lancashire and Yorkshire keener than ever it was before. As is usual with increased competi- tion everywhere somebody has to go to the wall, and in Northern Union football this is strikingly exemplified. Only the clubs with well- lined purses in charge of an efficient and enterpris- ing management have been able to keep their noses in the air, so to speak. Those which have been slow to act, have,to use another inelegant but expressive phrase, been going down the nick, steadily and surely. Undoubtedly Warrington is one of these unfortunate clubs. It has been unmistakably on the downgrade for a couple of seasons, and during the last eight months the edges of the " nick" have risen so high that the Warrington F.C. is in I imminent danger of being completely engulfed. A powerful effort is needed to haul the club out of the depths into which it has sunk, but the making of that effort is not a matter for consideration at this moment. It can wait until the annual meeting, or the entry of the season 1899-1903. Durine the seeson terminat- ing on Saturday next the Warrington Club has not had an eventful existence. Matches have been played, won, and lost,—mostly lost. The season started with a rattle, for on successive Saturdays Swinton and Oldham visited the Wilders- pool enclosure. A draw was the result of the first game, and a defeat by 9 points the outcome of the second. The following Saturday St. Helens came to Warrington, and were the first victims to the home team's prowess. These three matches gave onlookers a pretty good idea of what the fortunes of the Club in succeeding fixtures were likely to be.lt WAS apparent that the first team was not really strong in any one department, and the success in future matches was variable. Several changes in the composition of the home side were early found necessary, Boscow and ft Bate giving poor satisfaction at full-back and half- back respectively,and both being dropped early on. Hallam took the rear position, and Ashurst part- nered the imimitable " Smack " Bate behind the scrimmage, these two players filling their respec- tive places with credit for almost the whole of the season. In the three-quarter line frequent changes have been made. Holcroft was the first man to be tried, and on the wing he played some very good games, but ultimately lost confidence, and with it his place. After much cast- ing about a promising man was discovered in the person of Fish, Lostock Gralam, and this player was secured with commendable promptness. He soon proved his worth,and after scoring a try in his first match with Warrington, obtained points in nearly every engagement. As a foatballer he is the best man Warrington have tried this season,but his distaste for work ultimately got him into trouble, and for the last six weeks he has been suspended. When about half the fixtures had been got tnrough , another smart wing player was discovered in the town, viz. Harris, Latchford Rangers, and he too made a most successful debut, and bids fair with proper training to make a very usefal player. Thus tor a time toe Warrington three-quarter line was fairly efficient and if it could only have been kept as then constituted a better record might be behind the club. Paring the whole of the playing period, the club was seeking, somewhat leisurely it is to be feared, for players in other parts. Wales was exploited, and just before the cup-ties a couple of Welsh backs were secured. One had a big re- putation in his own district, but here he entirely failed to fulfil expectations,and C Wood as a centre can be marked down a failure. Wilcox, the Ebbw Vale half-back has done better, and may yet prove his worth to the club. Neither however are great "catches." D Aorrison, the best of last year's for- wards, was ultimately brought back from Dalton- in-Furness, where he had returned, and has since been a most energetic and valuable player. This about exhausts the list of new players who have been considered of much value as recruits and it must be admitted that at no period has the club been represented by a really capable team. The efforts at improving it, and remedying weakn4sses, have been very feeble and by no means creditable to the Committee as a Board of Management. All this work will have to be gone over again,for the Warrington F.C., to make a matter of fact statementecannot put a team in the field to-day which is one whit better than that which started the 1893-99 season eight months ago. Furthermore the attendance of spectators at matches has fallen off very appreciably, with the deplorable result that the Club has lost a consider- able sum of money on the year's working. Of late things have gone so rapidly from bad to worse, that the crowd, fond of football as it is, would not pay to see Warrington play, and the number pr isent at recent matches has been lamentably small. The early knock-out in the cup ties, when Oldham administered the coup-de-grace, gave many adherents their quietus tor tills season at any rate. There is scarcely a redeeming' feature of the season's work, unless it be the consistent good form of the" " tea,m,though that, has been marred by the loss of the championship. In the Lancashire Senior Competition one point more than last year has been gained, but the prestige of the club has been lowered for it now occupies tee sixth place from the bottom, instead of the eighth as was the case a year ago. div.head: STACK F/RE AT ANTROBUS._
div.p: STACK F/RE AT ANTROBUS._

Information was received at the Fire Station, Northwimshortly before twelve o'clock on Sun,' ay morning, that a fire had broke out in the stackyard of Old Pole Farm, Antrobus. mid-way between Northwich and Warrington. It appears that about eleven o'clock, when one of the farm employ 6 was attending to his ordinaiy duties, he noticed that a corn stack was ablaze. An alarm was raised, and Mr. loud a neighbouring farmer, quickly mounted a horse and rode to NortCwich for i he Fire Brigade. The bell was rung, and in about four minutes the members of the brigade, under the command of Superintendent Arrowsraith, who were atten ling service at the United Methodist Free Church ad- joining, were on their way to the scene of the c flagration with the engine, drawn by a couple of horses. On arrival at A.ntrobus—a distance of about six miles—twenty minutes after the alarm bell firs', ring, the brigade found that the fire was confined to two stacks, hay and corn. A plentiful supply of water was obtainable from a pit close by, and as there was a strong wind blowing the brigade first of all turned their attention to preventing the fire spreading to a nu.r.ber of stacks close by, and also a shippon. After playing on the flames for about two hours the brigade succeeded in subduing them. but they remained on the premises later for fear of a farther outbreak. how the fire originatel is at present a mystery. The damage, which is e.etimatel at about £lOO, is fully covered by insurance.

div.head: Wul ARTIST AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: Wul ARTIST AT WARRINGTON.

Those who attended the illustrated lecture in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Tuesday *von- ing, by Mi. Rene Bull, war artist and correspondent to" Black and White," were enabled to realise more fully than has been passible, heretofore the glories and horrors of war. It but required to hear the boom of shot and shell t) make the scene entirely r4alistic. Mr. Bull served his newspaper during the West Indian frontier troubles, and the more recent Soudan campaiga, with it historic battles of Atbara ' and Omdurman. By means of over 200 lime-light photographs, he was able to bring to the eye of his audience, the most important events which charac- terised both campaigns. The photographs were unique in many respects, some taken as they were ' under fire on the battlefield, and considering the difficulties which were encountere I, it 13 surprising that Mr. Bull has been able to bring 11.3 me such ex- cellent negatives. In the course of a few introduc-. tory remarks, he discounted the idea that he was delivering a lecture. Lecturers he said, spoke of what they saw and sometimes of what they did not see. (Lauzhter.) His I -Tturer, was his trusty and faithful camera, waich had no imagination, and therefore could not lie. What it dhowed it saw, and what it did not see it didn't record. The pictures shown were intensely interesting, and Mr. Bull's explana'ory remarks were punctuated by the ap- plause of the audience, who were warm in their de- monstrations of appreciatiln of the exploits of the heroes aril various detachments who distinguished themselves in the camoaign under notice. Mr. Bull introduced a voin of humour into his remarks, but his enunciation at times was et fault, and a portion of the audience tailed to catch what was said. The pictures, however, sp ,ke for themselves, and al- though a few of them were a trifle blood curdling, they weie the best of their kind we have yet seen.

SOME Liberals feel very 'The Old-Age Pensions strongly that they ought Inquiry. not to take any part in the third inquiry rhich has been resolved upon, and they can makE out a very plausible case. They ontend that the party which gains a marked Political advartage from the use of a particular "Cry" ought to be competent to legislate upon it, Without so natny searches after a scheme. They say that the simplicity of the matter, as pre- sented to the constituencies, has proved to be a delusion and a snare, and that after the most ex- haustive examination of every scheme presented We are in no better position than we were before. Why, then, it is asked, should Liberal members onsent to serve on a Committee which is to "me to the rescue of the Government, treat the question as if it were only a branch of poor relief, and enable the schemes of tuionists to be mixed up and then remade, in or- (ler to save the Ministry frem the disappointment Of its own followers? We can find no ready an- 31ver to these arguments. Even the need for in- quiry is in a different position now that the 4orernment does not scruple to say that it may ft.g;est a measure before the Committee reports, alld take its own line altogether. But, upon ma- ture consideration, we hardly think it would be Veisb for Liberals to show so much res3ntrnent and to hold aloof. They have always manifested a de- sire to promote the relief of old age, by pensions,or better out-relief, or by easier means of insurance; 'and if they refused to serve on the Committee it Would make a bad impression on the country, un- it c0u1,4 be said that the Liberals had a scheme 'of their own, ready to bring in the moment they Were restored to the Treasury Benches. There i 11,0 evidence of the existence of any such scheme. It is said that the President of the Local Govern- Inent Board is to be chairman of the Committee. l'his is quite right and proper. The in- quiry is about the "aged and deserving poor," an.cl therefore it becomes a branch of poor-law in- -I:.estlgation. It must be conducted under the 4.lght of the best facts obtainable as to the work- of the poor-law as it affects the aged, indoor and outdoor. The authors of the bills before Parliament ought not to be on the Committee, and few other persons have given much time to the .B..t,ndY of the subject. Wo are almost .afraid that .t 4 Te primary object of the Committee is to pacify .e hundred Unionists who signed the memorial .fancluding the authors of the several schemes be- ore the House. The inquiry may still have a 'arious value,and clear the way to a better classifi- cation of the aged inmates of workhouses,and the Ino,c)re humane treatment of the poor compelled to tain outdoor relief. But the pension policy has ts,waYs meant a good deal more than this, and it .e as intended to take effect more generally, much arlier in life; and to avert the necessity for real
poor-relief at all. Probably all that any mere in- quiry can do now, in the absence of Government proposals, is to cut the problem into two parts,and to begin with the poor-relief part of it first.

THE Powers to be invited to The invitstiens to the Peaceonference. the Peace Conference have C not yet been settled. There is almost as much uncertainty as there was a month or two ago, and some new complications have arisen. In the first instance the CZAR, as the originator of the Conference,issued invitations to the Great Powers, and most of them responded at once. There was a dispute between Italy and the POPE, the former intimating that it could not enter upon a Conference to which the POPE was invited to sand a representative, as if he were a Sovereign on the same terms as the other States. For the time this was settled by the CZAR decid- ing not to invit e the POPE to send a representa- tive. As soon as it was fixed that, the Con- ference should meet at The Hague the Dutch Government, in its character as host, decided that it had the right to issue invitations on its owe, account. We do not know what is the view of the Russian Government on the point,but we should have thought that the members of the Confer ence could only have been invited by Russia. It is possible, however, that there may be a ring of Great Powers, and an outer consultative ring of smaller Powers. However that may be, it is clear that the decision of the Dutch Government may become an embarrassment. Far inse;ance, the POPE may be invited by the QUEEN OF H A.retern to send a delegate. From the latest informatton this seems a rather likely proceeding. We alto- gether doubt its wisdom. The original idea was not an academic Peace Conference, but an earnest-, consultation between nations commanding armies and fleets, and vitally interested in reducing arma- ments and warlike expenditure. The POPE has neither army nor fleet. He cannot regard matters in the same way as Germany and France will do, and not even as Holland will do. Another European difficulty seems likely. Bulgaria was anxious to be present, and'R tigare3 t's claim was refused. The report now is that Bulgaria will be invited by Holland, subject to the assent of the SULTAN. SerVia has just as much right to be pre- sent, and probably will be so, as well as Roumania, both being independent monarchies. Nov there is a new difficulty. Russia does not want, probably this ceunzy does not want, to see the Transvaal Republic and the Orange Free State invited. The Dutch Press is quite excited on the point, and it thinks that invitations ought to be insisted upon, and should, in the first instance, have been made the condition precedent to the meeting of the Conference at The Hague. If Bulgaria, a vassal Power attends with the assent of the SULTAN, it is being asked, why should not the Transvaal attend with the assent of its suzerain Power, Great Bri- tain ? Probably an undue importance is being at- tached to th ese points, and the CZAR may claim a veto on all ',invitations to the inner and operative Conference. It seems to us that it ought to be so, if friction is to be avoided, and what was intended to be a practical and useful gathering is not to be converted into a congress of the wandering and irreaponsible type.

Mr. Edmund GOSSe'S delightful article upon " Orion " Horne, who flashes so meteorically across the pages of the Browning-Barrett cor- respondence, will recall to the public mind one of the strangest " curiosities of literature," who de- served a better fate than entire obliv.on. Horne was a fat little person—like an operatic Lord Chancellor—full of boisterous spirits and an un- limited capacity for exaggeration. He was so vain that late in life he would dance a breakdown at a 'wedding in order to take the eyes of the guests off the bride and bridegroom and attract them to himself. At seventy he could —and did—swim faster than many profes- sionals. The top of his head was bald, and there was the strangest crown of milky ring- lets that ever saluted a spectator's gaze. His tactlessness offended every second person he came into contact with, and yet he managed to retain the sincere friendship of men like Browning,Tenny- son, Leigh Hunt, and Carlyle, who declared that "the fire of the stars was in the man." For seven years of his long life—he snowballed the poet Keats when he was a lad, and did not die till 1884 —Horne was in truth an inspired and really re- markable writer. For more than forty years after he was a scribbler of tiresome balderdash, scarcely good enough to secure entry in the "poets' corner" of an American newspaper. Mr. Geese does not suggest an explanation. The probability is that Horne was mad—a victim of vanity's delusions and a general staginess which had sucked the brain of all its sense and strength. Yet he is more than worth remembering for the sake of those seven years of poetic usefulness, as a well-edited selection of his works would plainly show.

Dr. Parker took the opportunity at a Cromwell tercentenaty gathering in the City Temple, of un- burdening himself of a few candid opinions in re- markably vigorous language. It was not so much about Cromwell that ho spoke, but about things in general which apparently weighed on his mind. In fact he hit out right and left, and we should imagine that one or two of his well-aimed blows landed in tender places. The famous preacher cen- sured Lord Rosebury for keeping racehorses, the Prince fcr card playing, and the Kaiser for avowed friendship with the Sultan. Abdul Hamid be unhesitatingly damned for his atroci- ties, burials in consecrated ground be anathe- mised, and "Popery in Protestantism" be con- demned in equally unmistakable terms. The rev. gentleman, it will he seen, covered a wide area of disputed territory in the course of his remarks, for what reason we do not exactly know, but as he does not usually say anything without reason we are prepared to accept his tirade from the pulpit as on effort which was called for in some way. Ono of Dr. Parker's opening remarks: "I want living Cromwells, livin righteousness, living obedience to the law of God," perhaps explains as much as anything else, the line of oratory ho took.

The annual report of the Registrar-General is! always an interesting document despite the fact I that it abounds in statistics of the most prosaic I kind. There are many suggestive facts in the report just issued for the year 1897. It appears that Lancashire holds the unenviable posi- tion of having the highest death-rate in the country, the number of deaths being 20.4 per thousand. On referring to the annual report of Dr. Gornall for 1897 we find that the death-rate for the Borough was 19.5 per thousand, so that Warrington comes out of the average very creditably. Eateric fever is attributed by the Registrar General as a most potent factor in keep- ing the death-rate of Lancashire at such a high rate. As far as can be inferred from available statistics, nearly all the . thirty registra- tion distrcts in Lancashire are subject either to constantly excessive incidence or to frequent outbreaks of enteric fever. Warrington is nut down as one of the districts which are found to suffer least, or least freTrently from enteric fever. The number of cases notified in the Borough was 41 in 1897, as against 34 in 1893, or an increase of 7. In referring to this in- crease, the Medical Officer of Health wrote at the time that the largest number of cases had occurred in Howley Ward, "whore the usual associations of fever, viz, filth and filthy habits with overcrowd- ing exist."
Probably no one would care to argue,even for the sake of argument, that the huge advertisement of somebody's pills, ad somebody else's cycl

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY APRIL 28, 1899. RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY APRIL 28, 1899. RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

saddles which we see all over the country, are an ornament to the landscape. They certainly are not, and the promoters of, the Rural Advertisements Bill, which is to be re-introduced into Parliament, are very likely of the same opinion. It is sought to pre- vent the farmer and landowner from letting his land for purposes which so offend the artistic spirit of the community. But, though the majority of us would rather be able to traverse a smiling country-side without encountering these un- couth hoardings and signs at every turn, we cannot get away frornthe fact that there is much to be said in the farmer's favour, and even in support of the advertiser. Both have a liveli- hood to earn,and a profit to make like the majority of us, and they cannot altogether be blamed if their Way of making ends meet more comfortably does not not accord with our aesthetic tastes. Those who desire to check this defacement of so many of the pleasant places of the earth have every right to do so if they can, but they need not commence by reviling the farmer and landowner, , to the full extent of their volubility.

It seems to be a tendency of the age to grant rewards for courage and gallantry with a lavish hand, and the question arises as to whether the thing is not being carried too far. Of course no one would think of taking objection to a recogni- tion of bravery in its truest and highest sense, but when we find a desire to reward men for having only performed their duty under difficult circum- stances then we are forced to the conclusion that the honour is being cheapened thereby. The troops who performed so well in the late Soudan Cam- paign had a special medal struck in their honour, yet they had merely done their duty in an efficient manner. The Merchant Service Guild has recently applied to the Board of Trade for a reward on behalf of the officers and crew who so gallantly kept the Pavonia afloat until rescued. We are not sorry to note that the request has been refused. With all due respect to these courageous seamen we conteni that they only did what the service of their masters and the preser ation of their own liviatc: demanded. It s o lutely necessary, if the heroes of peace and war are to be honoured as they deserve for acts of voluntary heroism, that a distinction should be drawn between them. and the men who have acted with courage on occasions which come not infre- quently within the sphere of their duty.

The Californian who has written to a friend in Eagland complaining that he has to pay ..`3OO a year taxation in that State, although he is not by any means a wealthy man, appears so far as we can see to have a superficial grievance ; but it has nothing to do with taxation. He complains that he dares not sign his name to any letter running down the United States, for the letter would fled its way down to his locality again, and the local authorities would make things vary disagreeable for him. This is a new view altogether of the land of the free. Its citizens malign others, but will not suffer themselves to be maligned or even repr -Ached—a proposition so op- posed to American character that the Cali- fornian's complaint will probably be looked upon as the outcome of abnormal sensitiveness and very high taxation. The latter is not, it is true, pleasant for a Californian cit;zen to contemplate. Capital, instead of income, is taxed to its utmost capacity, and apparently in this particular case the taxation levied is steadily reducing the principal to such an extent that in the course of years there may be no more principal left to tax. In other parts of the country capitalists, small and large, are uttering the same complaint. It mty be well founded, but if it is so iniquitous as the capitalists suggest, how is it that they continue to increase their possessions,er even become capitalists at all

On Tuesday night, at a special meeting of the North- wich Urban Council, Mr. Williams reported that Sir John Brunner, the member for the Northwich Division, having been struck with the enormous improvements made in the old salt town, and the fact that there were still many ugly corners, had decided, in order to further encourage the love of the beautiful amongst the inhabi- tants, to place at the Urban Council's disposal £5O, for purchasing trees for planting in the streets.
