West-street, Widnes. Deceased was employed at Gossage's Works. Oct Friday, he was engaged in slinging lull barrels into a waggon in the company of James Coembes. Deceased was staading close to the end of the platform,endeavour- ing to pull a barrel which was standing on end toward him, who 1 his finger 3 lost their grip, and he over- balance i and fell into the wageon, a distance of 10ft., receiving a fractured skull. "NARROW ESCAPE OP A DRIVER."

On Monday, at noon, an alarming accident occurred on Savage's Bridge, Runcorn. A man In the employ of Mr. Earp, Preston Brook, had driven his master to the railway station, and was returning home whh the horse and trap when, just as he had reached Savage's Bridge. the wheel on the right-hand side suddenly collapsed and precipitated him on the pavement against the iron rails. Terrified by the accident, the horse dashed dowa the steep brow, and nothing looked more certain than that it would crash into Mr. Walter Collier's shop window: Sot just as the animal reabhsd the curb it slipped and fall with great force against the basement of the window one of its hind legs being trapped in a aperture over the cellar grid. The trap was a complete wreck. With great difficulty the horse was extricated,and it was then found that its leg was seriously injured. It was removed to Mr. Savage's stables close by, and the trap was gathered together and placed in the yard. The driver had a miraculous escape, and the wonder is how he escaped being thrown into the Bridgewater canal. It was fortanate that the road happened to be cleae at the time. A portion of the woodwork forming the frame of Mr. Collier's window was slightly damaged, but beyond this the premises escaped without injury. It is feared the injuries of the horse are sulh that it will have to be destroyed.

The monthly meeting of the Garibaldi Ledge was held on Saturday at the Blue Lion Inn, amongst those present being Bro John Bergess, grand meter; and lire John Brown, deputy grandmaster (Barlestown). Bro Joseph W Parry occupied the chair, and Bro Charles Chidlow,the vice-chair. After some portion of the business had been transacted, the Noble Grand (Bra Perry) called upon P G John Hughes to present a fratnel emblem of the order to PG James Atkinson for effi -.tient services rendered to the lodge as an officer. Bro Hughes said he was highly pleased to see that Bro Atkinson had re- covered from his serious illness. The presentation should have taken place two months ago. He had done his duty admirably, and hart gone through the chairs, and he hoped when the emblem adorned his house that it would encourage him to still promote the interests of the lodge. The secretary (P G Thomas Dickinson) also congratulated Bre Atkin- son, remarking that he was thankful to be con- nected with such a brother. Although he had not been very active in intro4acing members, he care- fully studied the rules, and acted upon them, and such members were. of the utmost value to the lodge. He honed that when the rules were altered he would give them the benefit of his advice. Bro Atkinson expressed his thankfulness to the lodge for the friends be had made, and promieed what he could do for it he would. The quarterly district report was then presented. After much discussion delegates were appointed for the Juvenile Com- mitte.e, and a voluntary banner subscription last was opened for the lodge members, being headed with a gift of one pound by one of the brethren who was accorded a hearty vote of thanks.

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.
A PROSPEROUS OUTLOOK.

Mr. Philip Speakman, C.C., president of the Runcorn Football Club, on Monday evening entertained the First and "A "teams at the Wilion Hotel, Bridge-street- The committee and other officers of the club were also present, and the company numbered ab-Jut 70. Mr. Speakman occupied the chair, and he was supported by Messrs F J Norman and T H Haddock (vice-presidents). . _ _ _

There were also present—Messrs W Cariolloklightbarn, W Jones, G Robinson, 3 Houghton (captain), G Wain- wright, C Pawns.ll (treasurer), George Garner, George Luirtou, P Deakin, J Clegg, George Msckie, S Abrams, A Rilcy, T Moores, A Roues, J Ellison (secretary), A Abel (assistant secretary), and others. The proprietor, Mr J R Ha%provided a substantial repast, and atter the tebles had been cleared, _ _ _

After the usual Royal toast had been put from the chair, and duly honoured Mr. Walter Jones gave" the health of Mr. Speakman, their president," observing they were all very pleasecrto have Mr. Speakman among them, and would be more pleased if they eould only see him a little pftener. Mr. Speakman had stood behind them now for some few years, and he boped they would have his support for years to come. (Hear, heir.) He was sure Mr. Speak- man was proud te be president of a club like Runcorn. They were as near an amateur club as any organization in the Northern Union. Moreover, they were all natives. (Hear, hear.) They did not obtain their players from up and down the country. With the ex- ception of two, all their players were bred and born in Runcorn. They did not go after players; they came to them. Mr. Speakman had cause to be proud of a club like Rencorn, which was second to none in the Northern Union. (Applause.) Mr. Lightburn supported the toast of the president's health. He could remember all their past presidents, but could safely say that from no one had they had the help they received from Mr. Speakman. (Applause.) He had been with them in their ups and dawns, and had stuck to them through prosperity and adversity. He was sure their president must be proud of the position ot the Runcorn club. They all knew he had helped them to that position, and if they had not had him to back them up. both with advice and financial help, there would not have been a club in exis-ence to-day. He thought the fact that they were an amateur team as near as they could possibly be accounted for their success. They played for the sake of their gooa old town, and it was this that had actuated the players more than any mem. tary gain. In conclusion he would like to thank Mr. Speakman for his hospitality. (Applause.) The toast was received with enthusiastic cheering and the singing of" He's a jolly good fellow." Mr. Speakman, in responding, said he felt he Tcould now claim them as his friends on account of the long time he had been a,societed with them. His connection with the Runcorn Football Club had beee one of the pleasures of his life. (Hear, hear.) Wherever he had been in the United Kingdom the Runco.n Football Club was known, and known as a first rate club. It had been truly said that the reason of their fame was because they were as nesr amateurs as they could possibly be. They were natives of the town, all working for one common end. They did not always succeed, and in this last season they had not kick, d as many goals as they would have liked. There was one goal he would have liked them to have obtained, and that was in connection with the Leigh match. (Hear, hear.) They would have been much better off if they had been successful there. He thought adversity was a very goad thing for everybody. If they were always winning nobody would play with teem. Some people lost the idea of sport because they allowed it to run away with them. In football of course they wanted to win when they paved, and they tried to win. He thought a great deal depended upon the character of the players in football. They knew the character of their players was formed by their associa- tion with the church and Sunday school. When they went away they brought back their characters with them. (Hear, hear) Wherever their lot might be cast they should see that they had such a character, that no one could pick a hole in it. Thsy did not occupy the position they desired this year, but they need not des. pair, they could go on trying. (Herr, hear.) His public engagements ani business took up so much of his time that he could not be with them frequently, but he could assure them one of the pleasures he looked forward to was meeting them under such circumstances as those to spend a social evening together. As long as they were willing to have him to preside over them his services would always be at their disposal. (A.pplsuse ) The Chairman next proposed "The town and trade of Runcorn." The town, he said, had had the same ex- perience as the football club. It had had many ups and downs, but he had good reason to believe tat it was now on the progressive path. He sincerely hoped that with all the different works that had settled in their midst, and the Ship Canal with its facilities—and he was glad to see there was a bridge that stopped some of the ves:els going to Menchester—he did hope taking everything into consideration, that Runcern had seen its worst days; in fact he knew it had; and he hoped that which had been lrgun so well would be continued in the interests of everybody who lived in Runcorn. (Applause.) HA coupled with the toast the name of Mr. Norman. (Applause.) The toast having been heartily received, Mr. Norman said he was glad that the time had now arrived when it was possible to respond to this toast without having to play the role of prophet or draw unduly on their stock of faith. Six years ago—with the Ship Canal just completed and the consequent transfer of many families to other localities—with their large works closing as many thoueht "Never to go again." it looked as if Runcern had" bat' its day" and it was only the most cheerful optimist who dared suggest that the cloud would speedily break and "the good old town" right itself again. (Applause.) To-day they had a very different prospect before them. To begin with he warned them against attaching undue impor- tance to the sensational report contained in that morning's papers. They might take it for granted that whenever if ever such a policy as that foreshadowed was decided on it would reach them through more official channels than that of an anonymous correspondent to the daily papers (Hear, hear and loud applause). The establishment of Castner Kellners at Weston Point, the introduction of such industries as white lead and metal extraction, the substantial development of the Old Quay together with the briskness of the shipbuilding yards, their foundry and their docks all pointed to the fact that the town had "touched the bottom" and that distinct signs of improvement were apoe.rent.Fle called their attention to the fact that his friend Mr. Imison in his financial state- ment to their local council was able to show a consider- able increase in the rateable value of the town. This meant the occupation of empty property which if steadily maintained would Down with the Rates" in a way eminently satisfactory to all con- cerned. No one in the town more fully apareciated the change than he did. During the depression he was hourly besieged with sad faces pleading for labour which it was impossible to provide (an experience which he trusted might never fall to his lot again). Now there was a reasonable opportunity of finding something to do for all who "had a mind to work." (Hear, hear.) With contented workmen and prosperous employers they might hope for happy times in the future. He need hardly say that all this would have a reflex action on their club. Their President had spoken of "ups and downs "in their past history. Was it unreasonable to suggest that these followed the course of trade in the town. If work was scarce naturally their good players would be driven further afield. while 'constant employment would increase the ranks of those from whom they drew their resruita. He was sure they would agree with him when he said that none had done more than their old friend Mr. Towns to build up the splendid reputation which their clubbed established. And now that prosperity had returned to the Old Quay, they would find the old interest revived. Assuming that he personally fell short of that standard of enthusiasm in the game that he ought to possess, they might be car: tam n that with two lieutenants such as Mr. Wainwright and Mr. Luxton the OH Quoy would be driven to give a good account of itself PSOPCiIIIV with the friendly rivalry of such foetnen as C,stner Kelner's, to challenge their title to supremacy. It was a pleasing sign of the times that employers were now taking an intelli- gent interest in the recreations of their workmen, and they would notice from the local papers that the directors of the ce:npany with which he had the honour to be connected were constantly demonstrating their ap- proval of such a policy, Their President had informed them of that as he viilled all parts of the country he was constantly gratified by hearing tribute paid to the splendid reputation of the Runcorn Club. He (Jr. Nattier') would close by reminding them that it was Perhaps even more difficult to maintain, than to estab- lish such a reputation and to this end they must apply their very best efforts. (epplause.) The Chairmae proposed the health of the Captain of- the club, Mr S Houghton. He said the name of Hough- ton was a household word wherever football was known. It was a great pleasure to propose his health, andehe trusted he would long be spared to be captain of the team, and interest himself in the club. The toast was received with musical hasours. Captain Houghton, in responding said he had played behind one of the best teams in the Northern Union this year. The committee had worked hand in hand with the players, and he malt coneratulate both the commit- tee -and players upon the success which had attended their efforts. He hoped they would stick together and haw, better luck next year. (Applause). The Chairman gave the toast of the sub-captain of the first team. J Butterworth. and the captain and sub- captaen -of the A team, T Warder and A Taylor. The toast was duly honoured. The Chairman also proposed "The committee and officers," coupled with the names of Mr W Carroll, the chairman, r C Pownell, treasurer, and Mr J Ellieon, secretary. The tout was heartily drank. Mr W Carrell, in reply, said the committee had done good work, because they felt they had a good loyal team behind them. (Applause.) Football clubs to-day could not be run without money; but it was an easy thing to run it club when they bad players who would tell them, as he had Wen told by more than one player,

that though the players had a perfect right to:have some remuneration, yet if it became a question of remunera- tion or no remuneration, they would play and uphold the e'andard of the club. He questioned whether they could find such another club in the Northern Union. To the spirit he credited the success of the Runc)ra Foot- ball Club. Well as the club had done in the past it had not seen its best. (Applause.) He believed they would achieve greater suocessei, especially with the support of such men as Mr Norman, to whom they were much in- debted. (Aopl ause.) Mr Pownall and Mr Ellison also respondel in approp- riate terms, as did the members of the committee, Messrs Lightburn and Mackie. During the evening a capital musical programme was sustained by the following : Messrs C Pownalla T Johnson, flppwood, E Worrall, A Grounis, whilst Mr W Grounds acted as accompaniar.

div.head: SAILOR. DR,)WNEO AT Virl'A'STON POINT.
div.p: A SAILOR. DR,)WNEO AT Virl'A'STON POINT.
THE CORONER AND "FORGETFUL PUBLICANS."

Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, bete an inqaest at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, las: Friday morning, on the body of Can Ostueos Halvossen who was drowned in the Manchester Ship Canal on the previous Tuesday evening. —Mr. Rosenberg represented the Weaver trustees, and Inspector Hicks represented the police. Crated Thyorsen, captain of the Schooner" Fred " testi- fied (through Mr. J. P. Carlson, dock-master, who inter- preted) that the deceased was about 28 years of age. Whist at Liverpool on the 18:h mat, he engage I the de- cease], and subsequently accompanied him t) Runcorn. When be met the man in Liverpool he was a lit:ls the worse for driak, but he gave him a shilling. They arrived in Runcorn at about 5 o'clock, by which time decease] had become somewhat sobered,and witness took him to Mr. Robert's shop (ship chandler. Percival's-lane) and gave him 43. with which to buy some necessary things. He instructed witness bow to find the ship and did not see him again alive. Deceased was an able- bodied seaman and a native of Parszund, Norway. Ole Sigursen, A. 8., said he WAS a native of the same place as the deceased. As he was on his way to his ship the " Como " about 9 o'clock Ira the evening he met deceased who was very drunk. He walked with him as far as his own ship, and left hint on the Quay side. As soon as he turned his back he heard shouting as of a man in the Canal, and turning saw the deceased in the Canal. He saw someone throw a line to him, but deceased did not take it. It woull appear as if the deceased failed to grasp it and sank. Witness was in the boat when: the body was recovered about half an hour afterwards. Means were resorted to to restore life, but were of no avail. Witness did net think that deceased Was capable of taking care of himself.—By the Police: Deceased was very druak bot he did not know whether he had a bottle with him. He (witness) had not seen him before, nor had he been drinking with him. Mr. Rosenberg, prod aced a plan of the Decks shewing where the accident occurred. He was of opinion that the man would be making for the Dock gates scion he fell in.

jotinjone', sailor of the" Dsuald and Doris " said he' was in bed on the schooner on the night of the 18th inst., when he heard a man shouting" schooner ahoy.' On going on deck he found the Captain of the sceociner had also come up, and they both saw the man in the water. Tee Captain to,d him to heave the man a line and he did so. The Captain himself want on the quay- . side and threw another rope. The man took no head of either and was drowned. He assisted in recevering tie body.—ln answer ts Mr. Rosenberg witness said the vessel was in the Dock at the time. Police-Constable Geerge B incroft, stationed at Weston Point. stated that about 5 minutes past ten on the 18th Inst. he was told by Sigursen(a previous witless) that there was a man in the water. On going to the dock he found they were just bringing the body out. He tried artificial respiration for about 2) minutes but with no effect. Subseqeently he examined tie body but there were no marks of violence uyin it. He found 14 21 on the deceased, but there was no evidence of kis having purchased anything in the shape of kit. As far as he could say the dccks were well lighted, there being lamps on both sides. At the soot vrhere the accident occurred there were no flints within'about ten yards. The Coroner observed that something had been done some years ago to get the flints away from the edge of the quay. so as to prevent any stepping on a raidA one and stumbling into the canal. Mr. Rosenberg said there was a wall cutting off the flints at tbat spot, and it was as the constable bad said, the flints were about ten yards away. Witness continuing s sid he had made enquiries of the Publicans in the neighbonrhoo I but no one seemed to know anything abouw serving a foreign sailor who was the worse for drink. The Coroner sail he never knew of a public-house keeper who did know anything of such men ; there was a wonderful lack of memory on toeir part when asked about such cases. Having summed up he advised the jury to bring in a verdic'; of "Found drowned." The jury concurred.
TIIEFT OF ROYtT.; A:r ituivuottN.
A REPEN rANT PRISONER.

Thomas Teelfer, boatman, Runcorn, was on Tdursday brought up, on remand, at the Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. John Oceleston, J.P., charged with stealing a coat, the property of Jo;eph Shallcross, captain of the boat " on the 18th day of April.—Joeeph Shall- cross stated he was the captain of the barge " Snafell " belonging to E lwerd Tyson, of Liverpool and Renc3ro. lie left his boat safely moored at the B )torn Locks pier head, ie the Menehester Ship Canal. On leaving he left the boat securely looked op. Oa going to the boat the following morning (the 19;h ot April) witness found the lid of the scuttle had been forced off and was left hang- ing by the lock. In the cabin he also found several spent matches, the bed had been turned -upside down and the coat (produce .) which witness had left safely on the bed the night before—was missing.—Patrick Cor- coraa, labourer, No. 9. Penketh-lane, Runcorn, stated, that on Tuesdey,the 1811 iest.,he was is the" Man at the Wheal " public-house. Church-street, Runcorn, in com- pany with his krather Michael and several others, when a man came in and said "Will any of you buy a coat?'" Witness said " Let us look at it," and he tried it on. Subsevently his brother Michael bought the coat for 61. The man Was a stranger to witnefe:—Mery Guy said she was a widow and resided at 9, Penketh-lene, Runcorn. The last witness lodged with per. On Tuesday night, the 18th April, his brother Michael bought a coat, and the following morning gave it to his brother Patrick, who wore it a few times. Oa Saturday, the 23rd April, P.C. Gregory called at the house, aed took the coat from behind the door. The coat produced was the same as the one which Michael Corcoran brought to her house on the 18th inst.—Police Constable Gregory gave evidence of going to thq house of the last witness at 9 p.m. on the 22nd Inst. He found the coat produced hanging behind the kitchen door, and took possession of it. Subsequently he eraminel the boat " Snafell" and found that the scuttle had evidently been broken open with the piece of iron, which fitted the impression made in the wood. He apprehended the prisoner in Halton-road at one p.m. on the 23rd April and on Sunday he charged him with breaking and entering the cabin of the" Snafell " sometime between 6 p.m. on Tuesday Ithe 18th inst., and 8 a.m. on the 19th Apricend stealing one coat the property of Joseph Shallcross. He replied "I know nothing about that." On Monday the 24th April witness went into the cell in company with Super- intendent Pearson wed saw the prisoner. fie bean t 3 cry and said "I may as well almit the lot, and I hooe you wilL have me dealt with here. I took the coat. found it on the bed, and gave it to a strange man the I same day that I met by the Welsh Row basin."—lt this stage prisoner cemplettly broke down and said from the dock" Have pity on me, I will never do it again; do try nee now."—TOO prisoner was further charged with stealing t.ti fetherne of meeilla rope, the property of Edward Tyson, from the" Snafell "on the 20th Apri'.— Joseph Shalicross stated he was clot tin of he beat " Sna Fell" (which belonged to Edward Fysin orLiver- pool and R ancorn), and resided at 16, White-s rest. Rene Irn. About 6 P.m. on Thursdey the 20h of Aoril Last, he left the boat which WAS thee lying in the Man- chester Ship Canal safely moored Tao rope pr educed was that with which he moored the beat, and which they celled a breast top He missed the rope the same time that he missed the coat. He valued the rape at 104. —Alfred Grounds, marine store dealer, Aehridge-street, Runcorn, stated that the prisoner called at his shop with the same rope about 3.30„ p.m. on the 21st April. Wit- ness looked it over and prisoner said "there are not any marks on it." Witness replied" I hope not ; for I don't want any stolen stuff here." Asked for his name he said "Thomas Trelfer, cantein of the fiat Sarah." Wit- ness found the rope was 20. b weight, and he gave the prisoner 9 i for it. He then left the shop—Police Con- stable Greeory, testified as to the recovery of the rope, from the last witneee. When the (constable apprehended the primer he questioned him about the roweand prisoner answered "I know nothing about any rope." Witness took him to the police station and showed him the rope and prisoner replied "0, I got teat from a man named Henry Green, who works on the fiat Sarah. He went up the canal en Friday and asked me to sell it for him. I sold it and got 9d for it. I gave him the 91. I did not receive any cemmis,ion." Witness failed to find any persoa of the name cf Green who worked on the boat Sarah, but there was such a boat. He subsequently ascertained that the rope belonged to Shallcross. On charging the prisoner with stealing it he replied, "I can't say. I did not !steel it. I sold it on Friday to Mr. Grounds for 93." The prisoner sub;e- guently admitted stealing the rope.—The prisoner's aged mother appealed to the mag:s,rete to be merciful for his poor old mother's sake--The prisoner again burst into tears, and begged Mr. Ockleston to deli with the case. —Mr. 0 tkleston said he had no power to deal with the case. If we could he would only be too glad to do so. The prisoner was committed for trial at the Quarter Sessions on both charges. The magistrates accepted bail, the prisoner to be bound over in £lO and two like sureties in each case.—Bail was forthcoming and prisoner was liberated.

div.p: RUNCORN CHARACTER, SKETCHES.

BY The gallery of our celebrities would b 3 incomplete indeed were the subject of &hi s week's re:narks not included in the eerie. Ile is tall,, rather lanky ; and walks along with a peculiar gait that is entirely his own. To most people he is a mystery—but there are others who know him well, or at least pretend to, though they are often left in such a irate of mind as not to know exactly what to make of him. He is gool natured, and " hail fellow well met "with alinest everyone. F3r this reason at times his intimate friends think they can score off him and make the brunt of their jokes fall upon him. Still he inevitably turns up smiling. He cannot be called a native—but has come—just come—though it looks as if he had Cottle to stay. Exesssively nervous and unrestive people are for ever disappearing and reappearing amongst the circles of their acquaintAnces, and this is a peculiarity that is exhibited in the above ease. For days together you might meet the individual at all turns, ' some- times ranning across him several times a day On other Occasions you might set out with the whole " local detective service " assisting you and end in a miserable failure as to where he " has gotten." Five minutes after the search is over—Hey! Presto! --Oar friend reappears. He is ever ready to spin you a yarn or crack you a joke ; bat he can every bit as easily "sample year clots "—end by the way he is a pretty good judge of the weed. He has never served upon any public body ex- cept possibly he might beep figured upon the wool- sack at the "Iroa Duke's Parliament," but if he has it is safe to say the honours of the post have been fully and creditably discharged.. When he is about, you my,'pick him up at his club, where his figure is always welcome. But . when be is on tininess bent. he wears a look lust as if he was anxioas to dispatch that and nothing else and he has a tendency to rush along from pillar to pose—ever at a pace that would brim.); utter dis- credit upon any of ear meesenger boys—in Pursuit of that " bit of biz "though he st39llas all the time to be utterly and indifferently disposed to get the busine is concluded ween he arrives face to face i with t. He is popular with the" lady section of the ce.mmunity ; and his excessive politeness to the opposite sex has gained for him the distinction of "the ladies man."

In musical circ.les he is always welcome and is ever ready and willing to give all the benefit of his vast knowledge of acoustics; and has rendered the town no little service in that respect. Be the company what it may he never appears out of place. If an odd man is required. if a party is in- complete, then it must be because our character has been excluded. Of what use to our town such a character might be? is a question not very easily answered; but who of 'is would say that Micawber was a character we did not love, if it wera only to teaeh 119 pitienca in "waiting for something to, turn up,"

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.

A POLICEMAN'S PERILOUS RIDE. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, before Mr. Monks (in the chair) and other magistrates, William Plinston was charged with having on the 14th April, at 8.35 p.m., hen drunk whilst in charge of a horse and Cart in Lovely-lane. He was further chare, d with furious drivinee—P.C. leoward said he was on duty in Lovely-lane at 8.35 on the night in question, when he saw the defendant driving towards him at the rate of from eleven to twelve miles an hour. There was no light or the cart. He shouted to the defendant to stop, but he took no notice of him, and drove on. Witness jumped into the cart from behind. and Plinston drove him all along the lane, and to his home in Ellen-street. off Bewsey-rcad. The defendant was drunk, and his face was Weeding. When defendant reached home he jumped out of the cart and ran into the house. The horse was a very wioked one and bit witness on the sleeve. It was very rough in the stable. —The Chief Constable : It was rather a perilous ride.— Percy Poole,ls.Hoyle•street. a lad, also gave evidence as to the defendan 'a furious drivir g. —The Chief Constable: Were you threatered by anyone tor coming here P—Wit- nese : No sir.—lt was explained that the witness); had been threatened by a woman, and the Chief Constable observed that that had nething to do with the defend- antlitThis was Ptinston's 49th appearance.—The Chair- man I We knew him before you did. The Chief Con- stable: I have no doubt; but I have known him as long as I require. He once killed a horse with furious driving. He is the most p-rfstent furious driver we have in Warrington.—The Chairman (to defendant) : You have only one neck, Plinston —Mr. Birchall And be will break it some day.—The Chairman (to defend- ant) : I don't know whether any warning will bo of use to you. It is a great pity to see you in the dock. You are a decent fellow when sober, but yru are as big a fool as there is in Warrington wthn you are drunk. I hope thTs will be a lesson to you. You will be fined 5s and costs in each case-253 in all. AN EARLY MORNING SCENE. Befote Mr. F. A. Frost, at the Narrington Occasional Court on Monday morning, a respectably dressed man named William Mason, Bridge-street. Golborne, was charged with having been found in the enclosed garden occupied by the Rev. John Themes Camm, Park-road, Golhorne, for an unlawfel purpose, with intent to com- mit a felony. on April 23rd.—Mr. E A White appeared for the presPcution, and informed the Bench that he pro. pored then only to give sufficient evidence to ask for a remand to Newton &slime. On Sunday mornirg shortly after midesight. Mr. and Mrs. Bennie and nurse (Mrs. Skelhorn) were in the sitting-room of their own house in Park-road, when they heard a noise from out-ide, Mr. Bennie and Mrs Skelhorn went outside, end the latter heard some peeple wrer ding. and on looking over the gar- den hedge into Mr. Camm's peen saw defendant lying fiat on his face on the ground. She called Mr. Bennie, who afterwards went into the house for a policeman's whistle. Prisoner got up, and ran away, but the nurse kept him in view. Mr. Benn,e came out of the house, and with the Rev, Mr. Brown, Conerega- tional minister. Hoy followed defendant. Mr. Brown caught him,and a severe struggle ensued, but eventually defendant was veured. He made conflicting state- ments, and said that he was going to Eatlestewn, then to Wiran. and after said be had just come out of the " Queen Anne " and that he had been to a football „Match and 'had never been in the garden at all. There were footprints en the soil in the garden which corres- ponded with the boats worn by defendant.—Mrs. Skel- horn stated that shortly after twelve o'clock on Sunday morning she heard a noise as if someone was scraping outside the window. Mr. Bennie and she went into the garden, and defendant was lying under the hedge divid• lug their house and Mr. Camm's. Mr. Bennie went for bis whistle whilst she watched defendant. The latter got up, went into the road, and ran round the nc:riier. witness" kept her eye" on him until Mr. Bennie came, when she pointed him out. Mr. Brown and Mr. Bennie gave chase, and subsequently witness followed, and found defendant in custody. She identified him as the man who was in the garden. She heard defendant say that he was walking quietly home,and they were insult- ing him —Defendant, who stated that he never was in the garden, was remanded to the Newton Sessions.—At these sessions prisoner was again brought up and the foregoing evidence was repeated. Mr. H. L. Riley who defended spoke of prisoner's previous good character and called evidence and the magistrates taking this into consideration dismissed the case. UNLICENSED CARRIAGE DRIVERS. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday before Mr. F. Monks and other magistrates, Edwin O'Toole, 7, Stoney-yard. was summoned for driving a conveyance plying for hire without a license. Detec- tive Barlow, hackney carriage inspector, stated that at a quarter to eight on Sunday, the 16th inst., he saw the defendant in charge of a 'bus and twe horses. As he was not a licensed driver witness told him that he would be reported, and he replied "You can do what you like." The defendant had told the manager of the Carriage Company that he was a licensed driver.—The Chief Ccnatable said the police were endeaving to stamp out this unlicensed driving because it was the cause of reckless driving. Defendant was fined 55. and costs.— William Cousene Goodenough, Wharf-street, was sum- moned for driving a hackney ea. He p e plying feit for hire without a license on April 15h ' Defendant was also summoned for plying for hire with an unlicensed carriage on the game date. Detective Barlow, assistant carriage inspector, said that at 9.30 on the 15th April he was in company with Detective Roper, when they saw defendant in charge of a horse and small waggonette. They saw a lady get into the vehicle. Defendant said he was driving to Walton. Witness asked the lady whether she had ordered defend- ant to drive her, and she replied in the negative. The fare was 23 to Higher Walton. The vehicle was not lieensed, and was not in a fit condition to be licensed. Defendant hired horses for the purpose of plying for hire. The Clerk (producing a document) : Thie is a memorial defendant is getting up from Stockton Heath fer people to say that he should ply for hire. The Chief Conetabie said there would te no difficulty in getting a license to drive, or a carriage license. if the applicant had a good character. Defendant had been to the court eleven times. Defendant : I never deserved in (Laughter.) They charged me with driving a horse 18 miles an h-ut and it would not go six miles an hour. (Langhter.) The magistrees fined defendant 54 and costa in eaah case. Defendant: lam very much obliged to pangentlemep. (Laughter.) I hope you will grant me a license and I shall he eaticfied. Crosfield ard Sons. Limited Warrineton. Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins defended prisoner• and pleaded guilty.—Mr. A. Browne,who prosecuted for

MvSrs. Crosfield, stated that prisoner was the traveller' for the firm its the Gainsboroagh and Lincoln district. There were three Penes nt accounerl for,vz , £1 12; 61 £7 14s 4d, and 17s 61. They had received a Ist of defal- cations, which amoueted to £l2O 12; 41, rom defendant by post. From Warrington, accounts had been sent to several firms in Gainsborough dastrict,but they had been returned with the inf,rmatioe that the money had been pail to prisoner. When prisoner received money he ought to have smt it te the firm's bankers the same night or to Warrington office. Prisoeer sent a letter to the firm stating that he had been compelled to' use the money he received in building up a business. His corn- mission had not exceeled £2 per week. Hi had not benefited by keeping tne money. He, expected trade to improve or he would have mentioned the matter before. He hid never done s sch a thing before in his 20 years' excierie.o.cs ae a traveller. There were a few pounds in e-oinmission- owing to prisoner.— Mr Jenkins stated that, prisoner had been engaged by Messrs U Cromfield, of Liverpool, for three years ; fi we years With the late Mayor of Manceester, and also with London tea merchants, before coming to the Warrington firm. The amounts mentioned woeld be relined when the firm made up the commission due to prisoner, but he had appropriated sums to his own use. Prisoner's com- mission was not acceunted for regularly, and he had been absolutely driven to use collected amounts until his commission was made up. He asked the magistrate whether this was not a case which might b 3 dealt with under the First Offenders' Act.—Mr.Breerne added that the commission amounted to About £lO or £l2.—The Chairman said they had carefully considered the case, and they •could not help saying that the frequent attempts to plunder Meisrs Crosfield from all sides was a very serioue matter and while there were strongly re- deeming features about the case they could not see their way to give him the benefit of the First Offeeder's Act. Prisoner would have to go to gaol for a month with hard abour.

AN OBSTRUCTION ON WARRINGTON BRlDGE.—Edward Green. 3, Brook-place, a carter, was charged with causing an obit:union on Warrington Bridge by allowing two horses and a lurry to stand thereon an unnecessary time —P.C. Chrimes stated that at 10.25 a.m. on the data in question, prisoners were standing on the footpath in front of the Central Station obstructing it. lie requested them to go away, but shortly afterwards they came back again.—The Chief Constable said defendants were station loiterers, and had beea up times out of number. A CONSCIENTIOUS ONJECToR.—AIfred Robbins was charged with a breach of the Vaccination Acts, 1867 and 1893, at Grappenhall, by not having had his child vaccinated —Mr. W. R. de Prez. stated the facts of the case, and informed the 'Bench that the child was born in October, 1895. and the delay in the present prosecution had arisen in eonsequenee of the defendant's changes of residence. Defendant said he was a conscientious objector but he did not pries his objec- tion on that occ talon although it was rather unfair that he should be compelled to vaccinate a four-year-old child.—De- fendant who pteaded guilty to the offence, was fined 10s and coats.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—WiIIiarn Harnblett and jlmes Hamblett were charged with haying been drunk and dis- orderly at Stockton Heath on the 3rd April. and on the evidence of P.C. Tarte were lined. James 2s 6d and William 5s and costs. _

No LIGHT ON HIS CART.—William Worrell was sumn-oned for using a cart on the highway at 10 50 on the night of the 19th April without a light. at Appleton. and was fined 5s in- cludinw costs.—Sergeant Gosling stated that the defendant drove very quietly alone the road.—Defendant said he had the lamp (now produced) in the cart. A candle wts inside the lamp. He did not see the police.—Sergeant Gosling: No, because you were driving so fast. _ - -

A BRA rE'WomAx.—Mich7tel McDermott. alias Michael Doherty, was charged with stealing a quantity of provisions, of the value of 2s, at Whitley, on the 7th April. the property of Dennis Doneghan. He was further charged with assault- ing Elizabeth Weir.—He pleaded guilty to the first charge. but not guilty to the second one.—The prisoner it appeared from the evidence, called at Mr. Frederick Weir's farm on the day in question. He was seen coming fro n the direc- tion of the " Irish house." He had in his possession some baton, tea, sugar and Bcc.. belonging to one of the men. Mrs. Weir endeavour,d to get the provisions fro_n him, when he assaulted her and attempted to strangle her. In answer to the Superintendent. Mrs. Weir said the prisoner had a knife In his possession, but he did not strike her. She did not know what he would hive done is her husband had not come up at the time. The man was very violeat and used bad language. I She had a long and severe struggle with him before assistance ' arrived.—Sergeant Gosling said he had known the prisoner five years. He was an idle, worthleis fellow and was a pest to the neighbourhood. He was in the habit of stealing the food from Irish houses and milking the 4:ows when he could do so without being seen, In the summer he slept in the fields all night. He had assaulted a lady cyclist. He had been in prison several times. He was really a pest to society. When he had money he went to Warrington "to booze it away." Other int3resting facts about the prisoner's career were given.and the Bench committed him to gaol for four months. The Bench complimented Mrs. Weir uron the firm- ness and courage she had displayed in the matter.—Mrs Weir : He has been to our place several times. I wanted him quite as much as you did. (Laughter)

INDECENT BEHAVIOUR IN TH STREET. —Joseph Game-, was was brought up in custody for not appearing in answer to a charge of indecently exposing his person in Main-street. Frodsliam on th 9 1-sth of January last.—Fe pleadel guilty to the once—The Case was proved by Police-Constable Price.—Fined 10! and 13s 6cl costs; DRUNK ON LICENSED P111115E3 AND ASSAULTING THE LANDLORD.—Tnonns spruce Was summoned by James Jack- son, landlord of the Wheat Sheaf Inn,for b-ing drunk and re- fusing to quit his house on the Ist of April last, and also with assaulting him at the same time and place—Spruce had taken out cro ‘s-surnmonses for assault.—Mr. Giles solicitor, Chester, appeared for Jackson. whilst Spruce conducted his own case.—Prom the evidence of James Jackson, juni , Wil- liam Sidles,. Henry Smith, and Frank Lamb all of Dunham Hill, it appeared that the defendant Thomas Spruce es.-ae into the Wheat Sheaf Inn, en the let of April the worse fo! liquor. The landlord re- fused to serve him, and tried to persuade him to leave the house. Spruce would not go and eventually the landlord (Jackson), took hold of Spruce by the col!ar and assisted him out. Upon reaching the door-step, however. Spruce turned round and hit him in the face.—Thomas Spruce,for his defence,called e.S. Inning and Samuel Wright. of Dunham Hill, in support of his contention that ho had been hit in the first iastance for nothing by the complainant. Jacksoa, and only struck back in self defence-- Samuel Wright stated that he saw no blows struck at all, and the Police °fiber's eridence reside' to show that Spruce. earlier on in the day, had had saffi dent drink to justify Jackson, the landlord, in refusing to serve him with more. The Benchdecided to dismiss th. case against Jackson, and fined Spruce, who it apneared had previously been convicted for similar offences, 21 and 21 lOs 6d costs, or in default one mouth's hard labour.
OPENING OF THE NEW RAGGED SCHOOL MISSION.

On Sunday evening the new Ragged School Mis- sion, Bank-street, was opened by a special service conducted by the Rev. Canon Willis, rector of War- ington. The building was form-irly used as a County Curt. The c3ngregstion was not very large, owing, perhips, to the inclemency of the weather, but there was a fair number of children present. During tile service special hymns were sung by the United Band of Hope choir, conducted by Mr. D. Fanshaw. In concluding his sermon, the Rector said much earnes..ness had been put into the work of various organizstions in Warrington of late years, and an example of their efforts could be • found in jhe beautiful rooms they mere then in. Another religious body was not to be formed in connection with the Mission, but it was for the purpose of bringing in the most degraded children. and subsequently, pass them on to the Church of Christ. Tilers was still much to be done. A large amount of money had been given by generous people. but £5OO more was needed to place the building out of debt. He trusted that when the building was out of debt the work would go on and pass into a higher and spiritual advr.ncement,using those blessed means which Christ had provided for them. Next Sunday evening a musical service will take place in the Mis Aon, and an address will be given by the Rev., F. E. Powell, vicar of St. James'.

div.head: MORECAMBE v. MILLOM.
div.p: MORECAMBE v. MILLOM.

This match was Waved on Wednesday, on the Salford ground, New Barns. berore a fair attendance of specta- tors. Morecambe finished the late season at the bottom of the first division table, wnilst Millom headed the second division. The clubs, therefore, in accordance with rule, played a test match to decide the relative positions that the clubs should occupy in the Lancashire Section next year—whether Minors; or Morecambe should be included in the senior competion. For three years in succession Morecambe have been the lowest scorers in the first division, and last year retained their place among the leading clubs by beating Barrow in a test match. Millotra,however, are a strong organisation, rnd the result of yesterday's match is that Morecambe are relegated to the szernad division and Millom gain admission to the first. The clubs were strongly repre- sented and the game in the first half was well contested, though Millom had the better of the exchanges and led at half time by one try (scred ty Northmore) to nil. In the second half Mom added a gull and two tries (by Young and Szniticlraro) atl adwn cire3 an uncon- verted try, (the first named club winning somewhat easily by one goal and three tries (eleven points) to Morecambe one try (three pins). The following were the teams :—Morecambe : 8 Thornton full back; H R Wilson, Altham, and J Bell, threequa.rter backs; R Belt and Wooilinuse, half backl; A Elkin, T Cornthwaite, A Wilson, Shm, P Wilson, Gowenloch, R Jackson and F Jickson, forwards. Mi;loin W Eagers, full back ; R Young, Whitehead, Leek, and Latham. threequarter backs; S Northmore and J Wharton, half- backs; E Knowles, J a Bucke-t,B Flogarth,J Smitheram, Fawcett. Grenfell, Scott,and Kitchen.forwards. Referee: M. F Renton (Hunslet). Trillel judges: Mr .1. H Houghton (St. Helens) and Mr J Underwood (Wigan).

div.head: FLETCHER RUSSEGS v. ROCHDALE RANGERS.
div.p: FLETCHER RUSSEGS v. ROCHDALE RANGERS.

These' teams met at Wilderspool on the Warrington Foothill ground in a contest for the championship of the Lancashire Junior L-ague. There was a strong wind blowing at the time. The t(ame were composed as rmlews :—Fletchnis : Knight, full back; Radford, Sut:on,Lawles,,Patrick,threequerters ; Feden and Scott' half back g ; Antrobus, Berry, F Berry, Jolley, Forster, Dayies.LoOker,Warburton,forwards. Rochdale Rangers: R. Schofield, full back; Hayes, Hickey, Mitchell, Ker- shaw, three-quarters ; J. Schofield. Hazekline, half hacks; Johnson, Taylor, Brooks, Dearden, Spencer, Hur,t, Bro Yen, Chaplin, forwards. The Rangers set the bsli in motion against the wind, and before a comoara.- riyely good "gate,' and immediately pressing play was teken into Fletcner'e quarter +, ad after two or three minutes struggle the Rangers grounded over their oppon- er,t,' line. 'rho kick for goal was successful. Nerved by this early reverse, Fletcher's lost no time, and forced the game in front of the Rangers' line and taking a pass Laaless scored in gool position. War- barroa made a good attempt tor goal. Continuing the pre&sere Sutton put in a fine run for Fletchera bat was brought down near tho line. Play settled in the Rangers' quarters for some time, Knight playing a capital gams. Lawless transferred to Patrick who tumbled the ball when near the line. Lawless a little later, again seeured possession and dashed away but missed a chance of scoting through not passing to Patrick. The succeeding play was of a mere even character. Knight made a ueeful mark and a sAmmageswas formed close to the Rangers' line. The ball was punted out of danger. Forster made a mark and Patrick made a dash for the line which as unsuc- cessful, but Radford got possession and crossed over at the opposite corner. Antrobus made a poer attempt for goal. The result at the interval was Fletchers 2 tries (6 pints) ; Rochdale Rangers 1 try 1 goal (5 points). On resumption of the game Fletchers pressed in the Rangers' half and the latter promptly forced play resistiesity to the other end where oight just managed to save a score by dropping OR the ball before the line. Play reverted to the opposite cerner where from a scrummage close to the line a Recadale half-back slipped over scoring for the Rangers. No goal resulted. A little later one of the visitors made a successful drop for Real. Sutton had to leave the field tarough injurics. Scott was very slow getting away with the ball and Fetchers missed many chances in consequence. Ferster went three-quarter hick at this juncture.a change which seemed to improy.t matters. Lawless secured and passed to Radfora who tracsierred to Forster and the latter

grounded after a splendid run. The goat kick was a tailure. 'Time "shortly came after this without any a dditicn to the score which was : Rochdale Rangers, 2 goals 2 tries (10) points ; Fletchers:3 tries (9 points).

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
LANCASIIIRE ALLIANCE. E4IRLEATOWN v. PARR.

Fresh from their victories over Adlins,,ton and Birken- head Locos Eirlestown turned out on Saturday confident of easily bagging another couple of valuable points. The weather at the outset was dull and threatening and the spectators did not turn up at Use Meanest Ground in as large numbers as was expected. The he:nesters were short of earr and Heyes was therefore drafted to the intermediate line, Mather making his first appearance for Earlratown at full back this searoa. Parr were fully represented and it was noticed that their ranks included " Cap " Lee, late of Earlestown. The visitors won ths toss and E srlettown were set to face the wird and slops in the first half, Hampson starting the game in the prefence of about 1,000 spectators. Parr were the first to show up, the right wing getting nicely down but Wilkinson had no difficulty in sending them to the right abont. Settle and Leach were next prominent with a some pretty plating, the form_r's centre being met by Smith who shot into the custodian's hands. *The ball was thrown away and fell at the feet of Sampson who tricked the backs and shot into the corner of the net after three minutes play. The homesters continued to have the best of matters and one shot of Hampson's just skimmed the crossbar. Aided by the strong wind the visitors becrine dangerous, the ball bobbing about in front of Chew for fully five minutes, the pressure being eventuatly relieved by oue of the visitara fouling Mather. No more scoring was done up the interval when the score stood: Ealrestown, 1; Parr, nil. The resumption Paw Earlestown going in rare style and the Parr defence early began to bustle about, first Hampton and then Leash trying shot., each of which were dealt with by the custodian. Toree more goals were added before the finifh, two by H unpsen and one by Smith, Eirlestowa thus running out easy winners by 4 seals to nil.

div.head: EARLESTOWN v. PRESCOT.
div.p: EARLESTOWN v. PRESCOT.

On Monday night Eirlestown journeyed to Pracot to p'ay off the return Alliance Brum with the club of that town. The result of the match was awaited with great interest in Earlestlwa as if Eirlestown won they were certain of the Alliance championship whereas if they lost they were bound to win their remaining match with Astley Bridge. After a fait and exciting gamel the re- sult was a draw of two goals each. Earlestown are now practically assur6d of the Championship of the Alliance as it has been announcepl that Haydock do not intend contesting it. They therefore meet a picked team of the Alliance tomorrow (Saturday), and the match is sure to prove a good one as the picked team is an excep;donally strong one. LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT COMBINATION.

div.head: NEWTON-LE WILLOWS v. EVERTON ALBION.
div.p: NEWTON-LE WILLOWS v. EVERTON ALBION.

After two previous disappointments, Egerton Albion sent word last week that they intended to play the turn match with Newton on Saturday. The first disap- pointment was when a telegram was received at the last momeat stating that the Albion were unable to raise a team, and the second wori was sent that they had dis- banded. They were, however, advised to try alai finish the season out and this they are going to do. Both teams were fully represented on Saturday and having lost the toss, Ellis set the ball in motion on behalf of the homes`ers 15 minueee late. A. couple of fouls close in gave Newton an opening but they were met by a sterling defensive, Again the homesters became dan- gerous and some exiting work in front of -MoD nigall was witnessed the ball eventually coming to the foot of Ellis who banged it into the net through a network of players after 15 minutes play. Rouged by this reverse the Athlone were roan clustering rhund Horrocks, and Morrisev wag forced to concede a fruitless corner. Half-time: Newton, 1 ; Everton Albion, nil. On the restart the home left were prominent with some grand combination' Frankland putting in a splendid centre, which rolled harmlesely along the goal mouth. Try as they would the Albions could not get the hall away, and Newton were soon again peppering the visiters goal, only the splendid goal- keeping of McDougall preventing a score. Just before the finish the Albions had a narrow escape. The ball was bobbing about in the goal mouth and Frankland obtained possession. This player banged the ball in,and McDougall caught it between his hands and the bar, the ball hanging there nntil the custodian got a proper grip. Whilst clearing, the goalkeeper was winded by a kick from Glynn. Final: Newton, 1; Everton Albion, nil.
WIGAN AND DISTRICT SRIELD. GOLBORNE v. BEIRTONWOOD.

• The replayed final tie in the above shield came off on the Mesnea Ground on Saturday. Both the men who were hurt in the previous match took pat, indeed Bun. her, the player who was unconscious for some time last week through colliding with the Go'borne custodian.did not seem any the worse for the accident. After a fast game in which they were far and away the better team, Golhorne were declared holder S of the shield by 3 goals to nil.,--Ifter the match the shield and medals were pre- sented by Mr. G. W. Stringer the secretary, of the Bar- lestown Football Club and the captain of the winning team walked to the Griffin Hotel with the shield held prominently In front of him.
WHALE-LIFE.
TaE ORPHAN'S FIRST BATTLE,

But now a time was fast approaching when our hero must needs meet his compeers in battle, if haply he might justify his claim to be a leader in his turn. For such is the custom of the cachalot. The young bulls each seek to feral a harem among the younger cows of the school, and having done so, they break off from the main band ard pursue their own independent way. TWs crisis in the career of the orphan had been imminent for some time, but now, in these untroutiled seas, it could no longer be delayed. Already several preliminary skirmishes had taken place with no definite results,aiad at last,one morning when the sea was like oil for smooth- ness, and bllzing like burnished gold under the fervent glare of tbe suri,two cut of the four young bulls attacked the crphan at once. All around lay the expectant brides ready t welcome the conqueror, while in solitary state the miehty leader held aloof, doubtles3 nandi7ating on the coming time when a mightier than he should arise and drive him from his proud pesicion iato lifelong exile. Straight for our hero' massive heal came his rivals, charging along the foaming surface like bluff-bowed torpedo rams. But as they converged upon him he also oh irged to meet them, settling slightly at the same time. Whether by accident or design I know not, but certainly the consequence of this move was that instea.d of their striking him they met one another over his back, the shock of their impact throwing their great heads out of the sea with a dull boom that might have been heard for a mile. Swiftly and gracefully the orphan turned head over flukes, rising on his back and clutching the nearest of his opponents by his pendulous under jaw. The fury of that assault was so great that the attacked one's jaw was wrenched sideways, until it remained at right angles to his body, leaving him for t'le rest of his lite sorely hampered in even the getting of food, but utterly incapable of ever again giving battle to one of his own species. Then rushing towards the other ag- gressor the victorious Warrier inverted his body into the sea, and brandishing his lethal flukes smote so doughtily upon his foe that the noise of those tremendous blows reverberated for leagues over the calm sea,wirile around the combatants the troubled waters were lashed into ridges and islets of snowy foam. Very soon was the battle over. Disheartened, sick, and exhausted, the disabled rival essayed to escape, settling stone-!ike until he lay like soare sunken wreck on the boulder-bestrewn sea-bed a hundred fathoms down. Slowly, but full of triumph, the convenor returned to the waiting school and, selecting six of the submissive cows, led them away without any attempt at hindrance on the part of trio ether two young hulls who had not joined in the fray. From " The Orpean." in the " Coruhill Magazine "for May.

div.head: ON BEING ALL RIGHT.
div.p: ON BEING ALL RIGHT.
Most of the male passengers kept saying, "We're all right. O'n yes, we're all right." But 'mere we?

That depends on what is meant by all right. We were not sinking, and there was no leak. Neither was the vessel on fire. The sea was now m oderate, and we rolled gently on it like rock-aby-babv-on the tree- t)p. Our bridge and fifty feet of our starblard railing had not been carried away, as they C 3 mmonly are in newspaper accounts of marine tr,oubles. We were right so far. But we could not be all right, becaus tie ship did not M 390 and we wanted to gat to Liverpnl. Tna enginfs ha -I not made a revolution in the last twelveihour3—a record easily beaten by any Smith American republic.

From the bowels of the ship cane a eaund of ham- mering and shouting, as if the big craft were suffering from some sort of congestion that was being treated sugc Lily without anwsthetics. Thera were lots to eat in the well-furnished Atlantic liner, but the people seemed to feel less enthusiasm than usual when the bugle tooted musically for meals. Conceding that we were making only about two knots an hour (all drift, and in the direction of Cape Town), the optimistic gentleman aforesaid continued t 3 urge the women not b worry, telling them we were all right. The mat morning the ship (as the American hoodlums tersely put it) " got a move on." A slow, dull move, though it was —ablut half speed at best, with intervals of stoppage, as if the surgeons were ad:ninistering to the machinery liberal desns of stimulants and beef t?a.

We arriv d at Liverpool nearly three days late, with, out having Icst a life or a leg. So far, again, we were right ; yEt not all right. Several passengers hal fretted themeelves into a state of nervous prostration,important appointments were missed, letters were delayed, and a hundred other things had got mixed and jumbled up. Now, my beloved :friends, it is not the ship or the man that goes limping and stubbing along—getting somewhere finally, in bad form, that is" all right." To be (11 right a fellow must do his work—all of his work— and keep up with the procession. How many of you are really all right ? Take an inventory of your stock and assets, and tell me. Here is Mr. J. A. Royston, of Sheffield. He was not all right; didn't pretend te le,. Yet, as he says, he managed to keep going, and under the cinumstances, was pardonably proud of that. He was all right up to October, 1887. Then came the e.reakdown. "At that time," 'ne says, " I began tn:feelitielvv,tired, and weak without understanding the 'reason why. At first I had a foul taste in the mouth, and my tongue was coated with a yellow fur. A deal of phlegm centinually gathered in my threat and mouth, which I was cons pelted te strain t o eject. "I had a sense of 'siekeess or nsueea, yet seldom actually threw up the conteets of the stomach. I did not relish my food at any ti:ne, and was often so sad against food as to be unable to eat anything at all. When I did eat a scanty meal the act was followed by pain and a sinking feeling at the'stoetech. " A hacking cough troubled and sheok'me, as if I had same ailment of the chest or limes. All my nights were more or less disturbed, and for works together I did not obtain more than three hours* sleep in twenty-four. I lost-flesh until I was two stem under my proper weight. Nevertheless, I strueglei on with my businese as best I could, and although never well,' I managed to keep going Sometimes a bit better, and then down again to my old level, yet never wing alwell day., I went on for fully ten years. No medicines I hal used in all that time did more than relieve me for the moment.

"Then on the recommendation of Mr. Clayton, the chemist at Wickir, I began using Moth or Seigel's Syrup It did me go ll within a wa'k. I clntinued uqin7 it' and steadily improvd. In less than a month I had no more pain, awl could oat anything I wanted, with no distress to come after. With my increasing strength the couh abtted, and soon ceassd altogether* In less than Fix nuaths after I to* the fint dose of Mother Seizes Syrup I had back my old weight, and with it the inieslribable and invaluable blesqing of perfect health. After ten years of pain and mental despondency from dyspepsia and liver complaint I was all i'ig ht at last. You are at liberty to print this letter if you like, and I will glAcilv anqwer any inquiries." (Signed) .1. A. RovsroN. 253, Infirmary-road, Sheffield, November 25, 1898

Mr. Royston is welliknown ad respected in Sheffield, when he has been in business many years. He was, away bank in 'BO, in the army, having served in the Afghan campaign with credit and honour. But his ill- -21°33 is of A much late r date,and probably was ia no way attributable to his experiences RS a Foldier. For his complaint makes more havoc in time of'pece than guns and sabres do in war. Tae3re is no mo,kiag a treaty with it that would be worth the paper and ink. As I have stid, few p?oole are " all right," but only partially rizht, aad the retson is more often dyspersia and liver ailmelt than anything else. Why, rowers Above ! I vvoader how any one of this world-full of dppeptics would feel if h were a,l•udly ail truly" a! right '' for a we2k. Let hilt try Mothtr Seigel's Syrup and find out.

div.head: RHODESIA.
div.p: RHODESIA.

During the past week public interest has continued in the Rh7desian share market, and there has been a rise in the price of nearly everything Rhodesian. Mr. Cecil In,adea has said that he is determined that the railway from Buluwaym northwards, to connec,.; with the direct line to Cairo, shall go on, whatever happens. Chap transport being thus assured in Rhoiesia, there ia every, prospect of the shares of the Austen (Gwelo) Develop- ment Syndicate, Limited, advancing to a very consider- anle premium. The Austen (Gmelo) Development Syndi- cate, L,rnitel, with a capitalof only' £50,000 in £1 fully- paid shares, owns a farm of 6.000 acres, and also 507 claims in the best known and most important gold mining distr;cts of Rhodesia. A number of the claims contain ancient workin/s, and are close to some of the best proved gold mines in Rhoc'.eiia. One of the largest financial corporations in London has already placed the whole of the workincr capital, which is £20,000. The shares have been bought during the past week by some of the largi firms, and at tie present priee of about 12,. 61. per share, at which the £1 fully-paid :tares are now der.lt in on the London Stock Exchange, they rergilt to be eeell worth the attention of tho. snoculative investor. (From " The Mining World," April 23, 1809 )

Sir,—A letter -appearing in your issue of April 15th, above the signature of Mr J C Sutton, Clerk to the Rural astrict Council, seems to require further notice from me: I acknowledge its conciiiatory tone and admirs Mr Sutton's tact. Mr. Sutton is jealous of the honour of the Rural Dis- trict Council, aud the procedure of his department,— loyal and laudable feeling on his part. In my opinion he would have bel,tsr ealeguarded theso interests it he had given the explanation (now so tardily Owe), at tneir last monthly meeting. aad so have prevented that bear uarden scsne which remains a die;grace to those parties who consider howling down an opponent fair argument. We seem to have established the fact that the figures £26 odd and £3B 63 31 did exist in toe books, a difference of 48 per c3nt, which certainly needed explanation. Wnen the figures were copied from the books at Mr. Sutton's office by an overseer, this explana- tion was asked for, and the answer given was so ridicu lons that it is doubti lif it was given serioualy. Again we were informed in public ineet!ng by the indefatigable Unairman of the Parisn Council that he had three times visited Mr. Sutton's office for explanation, and each time received a nifferent sat of figures. Under the cir- cumstances I did not exceed the bounds co fair criticism in orawing my own inferences and using them. Lat-r at the Rural Di,trict meeting (vide local press reports) it was suggest:el that the difference was made up by sewer- age chargee, salaries, commissions, etc. Now after this long interval we nave another, and what I take to he duly authorz d statement made by the Clerk to the Courscil, i s., that the £3B 63 3d included two o,s bills, with bills relating to the election of Parish Councillors, and a contested ilectioa for Rural District Ccunciilor. Wpy in the name of common sense all this hesitancy, this beating about he bush. Mr. Sutton with hatural modesty does not give details, at least of the expenses of the election of Parish Councillors (uncontested), or the ratepayers would see how rates are frittered away for practically no service rendered. It is very unkind of Mr. Sutton b take Us over 6 years' figures to prove us £36 in debt, and it is even worse for him not to eive us the other account on which we have overpaid £l7 odd. We care not,.it is beside the ques- tion. We have hsnourably met every call up to date.

It is a new exuerienci to hien to have chrie accounti questioned by a Rural District and the novelty has upset his stolidity. We are, again reminded that the Rural Dirrict G)uncil's accounts must be kept in prescr bed form, interring that no further interest ne d be taken.- Well, I pnetimo these accowits wero kept in this pro_ scribed form, met the usual requiremlnts of the Govern nient Auditor, and all was serene. Did they ? I merely ask the (very ? or, did this very tern of £3B El;. 3j. have the auditor's red ink pen drawn through it because tit inclu led charges which ought not to figure as spocia axpenses (although pod: ctly logiilmat,3 as charges against th 6 'offish). If so, where can we look for per- ectian ; " Co err is human." I for one do no bellevt that Parish Overseers Fxist simply to levy and collect the rate. I believe they have a. further duty, i e., the protection of the interest of the ratepayers against undue extravagance.—Yours faith- fully, Padgati.

Now in return for all this, can the following favour be too much to ask our ministers for ? namely, that they on their part, reciprocate this spontaneous proof of the loyalty of their members, not merely by praising us,but by showing us that they really appreciate it, by removing the grievance we have so Ong and so bitterly complained of, cansed by them in- eiseng upon nominating every one of our church officials, which places every laym In wishful to serve the church officially, entirely and too often abjectly, at the mercy of the minister. Toe redress we ask for is that the nlombers of the leaders' and quarterly meetings should have a joint right wita the minister in nominating me stewards or lay officers, they still retaining toe same right to nominate they have at present, as no one wishes to curtail their p.ivileges. Tait is virtually our position now, for it is cram that without lay noinsuatimo we can enjoy no freedom and no lioerty of actin, and no lay representation worth the uaine. E /en in the Essablisned Church the laity hay:, a right of notniaating bait the war lens or stewards. We cannot but reeret that our ministers suoalu insist upon retain- ing tots arbitrary power in their owl baud;, thus pre- venting us from exercising a right euj veo by me lay- ale..l in every Protestant Cnurch in the land except our own. . _ .

1 now appeal to all Wesleyans who lova their church to assist us in removing tnis grievance ; it not for your ova sakes,do so for tile sake of your children. If we do our duty now we may save mem from eadless strife, or ih)wevN* determined our ministers may be that flings shall continue as they .tre, tuey back the rising tide ct progress, advancing all around us (the very air is iul ot the sound oi and all contents are feeling its force in one form or another, either on questions of ritual, doctrine, 'o r forms of government. Shortly after five o'cleck on Sunday evening a Warrington craw had a thrilling experience in Menai Straits. Mr. Barnard, the general manager for Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sous, Bank Quay, is the ()watt of an 80-con schooner yacht named Rowena, fitted up for 12 or 14 persons, and it is cusomary for him to take a few employes of the firm for a cruise weekly. Mr. Bernard and party left Liverpool in the yacht at midnight on Satur- day for Bdaumaris, mad entered the Straits at dead low water. There being insufficient water outside the chaanel, which is very narrow, they anchored to wait for the rising tide, and whilst in that posi- tion a sudden squall sprung up from the south- eout,h-west, which developed into a strong gale. Whilst the crew were engaged in setting sail to escape from the position in which they found them- selves, the rocks of Puffin Island forming a danger- ous leeshore, the anchor chain parted, and before weigh could be got on tne vessel she struck a ledge of rooks connecting the parch with Puffin Island, and she immediately began to break over. Mr. Bernard, realizing that the vessel would in all probability break up, gave instructions to the Cap- tain to at once take measures to save the crew. The large dingey was then launched, and the Captain with tour hands, endeavoure I to make the shore of the island. After being nearly capsized, the diugey managed to reach the shore in safety. The boat was considerably damaged, and several of the crew were bruised and hurt by being thrown on the rocks by the heavy sea. After landing the four men, the Captain made strenuous efforts to get back to the ' rock to bring off the remainaer of the craw, but the , gale had by this time lashed up so heavy a sea that this proved impossible. The owner, seeing that he could not hope for help from his own boat, allowed distress signals to be shown. Those were immedi- ately answered at the lifeboat station at Penmon, rockets being fired and the signal hoisted to sum- mon the lifeboat crew. it was, however, an hour and twenty minutes before the beat could be launched. The boat at the end of that time made towards the yacht, with Sir Richard Belkeley at the helm. Mr. Bernard now realized the fact that the boat had not been broken ap, owing to the back set of the current pouring through the ledge from outside the Straits and rushing up with the full force of a strong flood tide. This peculiar action of the water had kept the vessel from crashing against the rocks. Entertain- ing some hope of saving the yacht, Mr. Bernard manceuvred the sails in such a manner that she would have a chance of heading off the rock,which she eventually did, and, slipping into deep water, stood away from the islanci, followed by tha life- boat. Being shorthanded, owing to the Captain and some of the crew having been landed on the island, he took on board a pilot and three men from the lifeboat and threshed up against the gale from Beaumaris The lifeboat returned to Puffin Island and rescued the party which had been landed there and then found itself in an awkward predicament. The sea was too heavy to permit the boat to return to Penmon, and the only alternatives were to go down to leeward to Conway, or to follow the yacht to Beaumaris. This Sir Richard Bulkeley decided to do, and after two houri battling to windward the lifeboat reached Beaumaris. On landing there the sea was so strong that she met with a mishap, et stem being broken against the pierhead as she was landing the passengers.

There were present: Revs T R Matthews, W H Drum- mond, Dr Patterson, Mrs Clay, Mrs Eielsten, Messrs Pilling, A J Jolley, T B Ashcroft, William Hickman, H Thornton, 9 Davies, J Billinge, William Hong ton, J Boil, A Brooks, T B Malkin, J W Knowles, T Halton. div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

It was decided that the Clerk should preside as tem- porary chairman during the election of Chairman of the Board. He said his only duty was to ask someone to nominate a chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. BALL proposed the name of Mr. A. J. Jolley and said he was sure everyone would be in favour of the proposition. Mr. J. W. litrowtms said he had very great pleasure in seconding toe proposition. Be hoped the motion would meet with the unanimous eupport of the members. Mr. G. PILLING, Mr. W. Houghton, Mr. Hibbert, Mr. Davies and Mr. Thornton suppered the proposition. Mr. Thornton ohserved that there were times and seasons "when men rufiie." He had watched Mr. Jolley's career during the time he had been a member of the Board, and he had found that he had acquitted himself honourably and had conducted the business fairly. The CLERK :: The motion is that Mr. A. J. Jolley be chairman for the rest of the century and for a part of 1900. (Laughter.) The motion having been heartily agreed to

- The CHAI i RMAN, n reply, said be tfiaaited them very sincerely fur the honour they had conferred upon him. ft was an honour which was particularly gratifying from the manner in which his name had been proposed, secon- ded and received.lle could not hope to rival his predeces- sor in tactfulness ; in matters of tha';.kind he was unap- proachable, but he hoped to deserve the confidence they had placed in him by maintaining unsullied the best traditions of the chair. When he remembered some of the men who had preceded him in that honourable posi- tion, he felt it would be impossible to carry wilt the duties adequately unleas he had the loyal support of the members ot the Board. The chair had been occupied in the past by euch man as Henry Bleckly, George Farrar Roberts, his (the chairman's father), Mr. jalley, and Mr. Sutton—and they were pleased to nave the last slimed with them still as clerk. (Hear, hoar.) Me folly rea- lised the difficulties which fell in his path if he was to follow worthily in their steps. (Applause.)

From information he received h 3 went to the Police Statieu at Lyanin, on toe 12ca hoot., and there sew a aueep which ice iclear.ified as belonging to Messrs. Singleton and Stephenson. He counted them on the 13;to inst and there were tuen only 825. On the eiguteeotte be resonated them and there were still three missing. He was coafident the sheep belonged to his employer: he knew them by the markings.—Tuomas Basnett, farmer, Acton Grange, near Warrington, said his larm was close by the BridAewater Canal. He dealt iu;provender for boat horses. On Monday night tne 10th inst., the prisoner Jones came to his tarna to buy some corn. After he had supplied him the prisoner asked him to come and see what they had got in the cabin. He went mere and saw a weep tied up with a piece of string in the cabin of one of the pair of narrow boats.--John Samuel Austin, butener, Bridgewater-street, Lynam, said on Tuesday toe 11th at 'nada no WAS in the snug at the Bridgewater Arms. Lymm. The prisoner James came in and said " I have pulled a sheep out Of We cut towards Run- corn." Ile offered to sell the sheep to witness for half a crown. Witness said" Why don't you advertise ; get ss. if you do. There's an office in Lynam where you can advertise." The prisoner said "All right I'll do so." The elder prisoner William came lac° the snug, but left the room several Limes and he didn't know wia.ther be heard toe coaveraation.—Police•Sergeant Garner of Lymin, said from intormatioo received on the afternoon ot tne 11ch inst. he went te Broadaeath and on the tow- ing path °lithe Bridgewater Canal be met the prisoner la charge of the na.trew boats " Hero " and Nero." which were sailing abreast in the direction of Manchester. Tue prisoner James was on toe towing path and admitted that tie teal a saeep on board. Witness found a white faced sheep in one of the cabins and he took pos- session of it. Re asked the prisoner to account for it, aril James said : " I hulled it out of the canal just this side Runcorn." He then askel where tuey were takiog it to and James replied" I don't know." He appreheu- ded the prisoner on suspicion of having stolen it, and at the Police Station, Lynam, formally coarged them with stealing the sneep. William replied " I've never pinched a sheep yet." James said" I have pulled it out of the canal."—P.C. Carrington, Runcorn, sp ?Ito to receiving the prisoner in custody at Lynam. On tee way back to Runcorn, the prisoners commenced CO talk about the mess they had gut themselves into. William said he had never Leached WS guest,. James said he WAS in toe cabin, having his tea waen his niece called out to him "There's a sheep in thecaaal." He jumped on the towing path near to the Greasi Bridge, bat could not reaela it. He then got on tee boat again and got into the park side of the canal and pulled it out. He took it into the cabin and wrapped it up in a rug. At Acton Bridge the same night.he snowed the sheep to a fariner.—lu cross- examination the prisoner James adnerecl to his state- ment that he ban rescued the sheep from the canal and called his father who when sworn confirmed the same statement.—Tne magistrates considered Were was not sufficient evidence to commit the prisoners for trial and discharged them. SHOW OF AZALEAS AT WA.L'reN LEA.

On Sunday and Monday afternoons, Councillor Crostield again threw his' grounds at Walton Lea open to the public to enable them to see his show of azaleas. Owing, however, to the unsettled state of the weather there was a small number of visitors each day, particularly on Monday, wnen probably n:)t more tuan 150 or 200 persons put in an eppe.ar- once. rue anleas, of which there were many varieties,and which were exhibited in the conserva- tory adjoining the house, were well worth seeing, indeed in the opinion of those competent to judge it was the best show Mr. Kipps, the head ganiener, has ever got together. In the same conservatory were also on vie iv a number of choice rhodoaen- drone and other flowers, and the whole presented an exquisite picture not easily to be forgotten. The camelias in the other houses were not at their best, but there were sufficient good verities left to give the visitor an excellent idea of what the shew was a few weeks ago. Orchids,flowers and fruits in other parts of the grounds were seen, and the visit afforded extreme pleasure to those who availed themselves of the opportunity.
